title: Plan Commission Meeting
overview: The Wausau Plan Commission met on October 20, 2026 and approved five action items, including the landmark designation of Yawkey Park, a rezoning at 909 South 60th Avenue from medium to heavy industrial, a preliminary plat for the West Hill First Addition subdivision, and two alley/road vacations. The Yawkey Park landmarking, supported by public comment from the Yawkey family heirs and a unanimous Historic Preservation Commission vote, will advance to City Council for final approval.

discussions.item: Public Comment – Yawkey Park Landmarking
discussions.body: Two speakers addressed the commission. Kathy Foley, 1209 East Hill Drive, read a statement on behalf of the Yawkey family heirs — great-grandchildren Alice Woodson Smith, A. Woodson Haigie, Abigail Spire, Lee Tuckey, and Nancy Lee Fischer — expressing full support for designating Yawkey Park as a historic landmark and calling for protection of its 106-year-old footprint 'deeded for use by the public in perpetuity.' Christine Martins, 1228 Arthur Street, noted she authored the nomination document and that the Historic Preservation Commission had already passed it unanimously with no opposition at the public hearing stage.

discussions.body: A motion to approve the September 15, 2026 minutes was made by Bruggeman and seconded by Balkin. No corrections were offered and the minutes were approved by voice vote.

discussions.item: Potential Landmarking of Yawkey Park (Item E, moved up)
discussions.body: The mayor moved this item up on the agenda to accommodate attending citizens. A motion to approve was made by Bruggeman and seconded by Balkin with no discussion. The commission approved the landmarking unanimously by voice vote; the mayor noted the measure would proceed to City Council for final action.

discussions.item: Rezoning of 909 South 60th Avenue – Medium Industrial to Heavy Industrial (Item 4A)
discussions.body: Assistant City Planner Edmonson explained that the parcel is surrounded by heavy industrial uses and natural features that buffer it from other development, and noted that a neighboring parcel to the north had recently received a similar rezoning. Staff found no concerns with the application and recommended approval as consistent with surrounding properties. The commission approved the rezoning unanimously by voice vote; the mayor confirmed it would go to November City Council.

discussions.item: West Hill First Addition Preliminary Plat (Item 4B)
discussions.body: Planner Lenz explained the preliminary plat covers a new subdivision west of Stettin Elementary School, with Arborvitae Drive designed to connect to the adjacent Greentree subdivision to the west. The INF Committee had previously recommended approval unanimously. The commission approved the preliminary plat unanimously; the developer will return with a final plat for the phase-one lots.

discussions.item: Vacating and Discontinuing Alley Bounded by Lakeview Drive, Bertha Street, Elmwood Boulevard, and Midway Boulevard (Item 4C)
discussions.body: The mayor described the alley as an unpaved grass strip with limited use and no garage access dependency. All adjacent property owners except 2514 signed a petition to vacate, and a utility easement would remain in place. The INF Committee had previously recommended approval. The commission approved the vacation unanimously by voice vote.

discussions.item: Vacating and Discontinuing 134-ft Southerly Extension of Liberty Ridgeway (Item 4D)
discussions.body: Commissioner Trueblood explained that Liberty Way continues to the east and north, making this southern stub an undeveloped dead end; a large home is being constructed in the area, making vacation appropriate. He stated he 'strongly advised' approval. A utility easement will remain. The commission approved the vacation unanimously by voice vote.

overview: The Village of Weston Tourism Commission met on October 20, 2025, acknowledging a strong summer tourism season highlighted by the World Horseshoe Tournament, which generated $3.2 million in direct visitor spending and $5.1 million in economic impact. Two grant requests — the 2026 Fall Cup post-event request and a tree-clearing project on the Eau Claire River — were tabled until the January 2027 meeting due to missing post-action reports and absent applicants. Several post-event reports were acknowledged and a suggestion was raised to require revenue/expense summaries in future post-event reporting.

discussions.body: Jim Pensel, 500 [street inaudible] Weston, raised two concerns: first, that the meeting packet layout was confusing; second, that a post-event request for the Fall Cup soccer event was submitted without a concurrent after-action report even though the event had already occurred. He also questioned the realism of room estimates in some applications, noting the Village of Weston only has 317 hotel rooms, and urged that future applications specify rooms impacted within Weston specifically.

discussions.item: September Budget Status Report
discussions.body: The commission acknowledged a budget status report showing revenues and expenditures through the second quarter. A member noted the account balance stood at $233,531. No questions were raised and the report was acknowledged by motion.

discussions.item: CVB Report
discussions.body: CVB representative Tim reported a highly successful summer tourism season, led by the World Horseshoe Tournament, which drew approximately 3,000 participants and families over two-plus weeks, generated $3.2 million in direct visitor spending and $5.1 million in economic impact, and brought hotel occupancy in the area to 86.2%. Tim noted discussions are underway with World Horseshoe leadership about potentially hosting again in 2033 and 2037 without a formal bid process. Marathon County's total annual tourism economic impact was cited at over $520 million with 2 million-plus visitors. Discussion also touched on the lack of new grant applications ahead of the upcoming funding cycle and whether posting meeting dates publicly on the CVB website would help applicants meet deadlines.

discussions.item: Grant Request — 2026 Fall Cup Post-Event Request
discussions.body: Commissioners noted applicant Dan was not present to explain the late submission. Tim confirmed the CVB had no communication from Dan regarding the application or his absence. Members expressed concern about setting a precedent by approving after-the-fact requests without adequate documentation, though several acknowledged the Fall Cup is a significant event. The commission voted unanimously to table the item until January, directing the CVB to contact Dan and require his presence at the next meeting along with a post-action report.

discussions.item: Grant Request — Clearing of Trees from Eau Claire River
discussions.body: The applicant was not present. One commissioner shared a personal account of a dangerous incident on the river caused by downed trees, supporting the safety rationale for the project, and noted the trees had already been cut. However, commissioners agreed they lacked sufficient detail — including how many trees were removed, photos, and a post-action report — to act. The item was tabled until January with a request for pictures and a full post-action report.

discussions.item: Post-Event Reports (Items 9A–9E): Wings over Wisconsin Wausau, Fourth of July, Weston Acoustic Concert Series, Bluesfest, World Horseshoe Tournament
discussions.body: Commissioners reviewed five post-event reports. Questions were raised about the Wings over Wisconsin Wausau report regarding what the 'value amount' column represented (clarified as marketing expenditures, not revenues) and whether the event's financials were disclosed. A suggestion was made to add a revenues-versus-expenses requirement to post-event reporting forms, with the chair directing this be placed as a separate action item for January. All five post-event reports were acknowledged by a single motion, passed unanimously.

discussions.item: Staff Remarks and Future Meeting
discussions.body: Staff reminded commissioners that a Halloween map is currently active for residents to submit Halloween activities, and that the end-of-year farmers market survey is open through October 30th. The next meeting was set for January 18th, 2027, at 4 p.m., with the two tabled grant items and a potential policy vote on post-event financial reporting to be added to the agenda.

title: Joint Budget Workshop Meeting
overview: The Village of Weston held a joint budget workshop with the Finance and Human Resources Committee and Board of Trustees to review the proposed 2027 budget across all funds and make key decisions on refuse fees and the public hearing notice. The board approved a $30 increase in annual garbage fees (raising the rate to $235.50) for 2027, with plans to re-evaluate annually, and approved the public hearing notice for the 2027 budget with a 5-2 vote. A projected 8-cent decrease in the tax rate was noted, though a future reassessment of all village properties is anticipated as the assessment ratio has fallen below required thresholds.

discussions.body: Jim Johnson of 5000 Street, Weston, addressed the board on several concerns. He argued that the refuse reserve fund would be depleted within months and criticized the village for not billing the Town of Weston its approximately $100,000 share of fuel surcharges, calling it the result of 'Maloney's handshake deals from the 90s.' He also challenged a budget slide showing a tax rate decrease, saying it was misleading because it reflected a property revaluation rather than reduced spending, and questioned why the Mountain Bay Metro Police Department budget showed a 4.63% increase when their oversight board approved less than 3%.

discussions.item: 2027 Budget — Tax Rate and General Fund Review
discussions.body: Finance Director Jessica presented the proposed 2027 budget, noting the projected tax rate decrease had shifted from 10 cents to approximately 8 cents after updated assessment ratio data arrived on Friday. She explained the village's assessment ratio has dropped to 0.86, triggering a future mandatory reassessment, likely within a few years. Extended discussion covered the Mountain Bay PD budget showing a 4.63% increase, which staff explained was an artifact of the way $100,000 was moved from the capital fund to the general fund in 2026, not an actual contract overage. Trustee Ermeling raised numerous line-item questions including overtime in committee budgets, ice rink wages, pet licensing pass-throughs, DPW salary transfers back from TIFF, and the street operations bonus line of $66,000, which staff confirmed was the transportation aid increase discussed at the prior meeting and part of the approved compensation plan.

discussions.item: 2027 Budget — Debt and Borrowing Discussion
discussions.body: Trustees raised significant concerns about the village's total debt load. Trustee Beck pressed staff to confirm whether the $4 million bank note for the Mountain Bay police building was included in Ellers' projected combined principal of $49,380,132, expressing concern the real total could be $53-54 million. Staff confirmed the $4 million was included in Ellers' figures after a trustee found the notation in the orange header of Table 9. Jessica clarified total village outstanding debt is approximately $55 million at end of 2026 when revenue bonds are included. Trustees requested a review of the village's debt policy, last updated in May 2008, be placed on a future agenda. A trustee also recommended the board formally approve loan covenants for the $4 million police building bank note, which staff agreed to bring back for board review.

discussions.item: 2027 Budget — Special Revenue, Capital, and Utilities
discussions.body: Discussion of special revenue funds included TIFF 1 closure with approximately $1.5 million anticipated to be allocated to taxing districts pending audit completion, and TIFF 2 remaining open as the deficit is not yet paid off. Room tax fund discussion prompted a trustee to suggest a dedicated future meeting to discuss allowable uses for tourism revenue beyond the current split between the CVB and transfers to the aquatic center and capital equipment fund. On utilities, staff noted a sanitary sewer rate increase will be needed in 2027, with Finance noting the remote metro sewage district costs have risen nearly $1 million over the past decade and are difficult to predict. Pool leak detection was reported ongoing since October 8th with results still pending.

discussions.item: Refuse and Recycling Fund — Garbage Fee Increase (Item 9)
discussions.body: Staff presented options for annual garbage fee increases, with a $30 increase (to $235.50) included in the proposed budget. The estimated year-end fund balance is $62,400 before any rate change. Public commenter Jim Johnson's earlier argument that the Town of Weston should be billed its share of fuel surcharges (approximately 4% of total costs, estimated at $100,000 for 2026) was addressed; staff clarified the town pays the same per-unit rate as village residents and is billed accordingly. After discussion, Finance Committee member Rickert moved to increase the fee to $235.50 for 2027 only, with re-evaluation in future years. The motion passed unanimously in committee and was adopted by the board, with Trustee Olson voting nay.

discussions.item: 2027 Budget Public Hearing Notice (Item 10)
discussions.body: Staff presented the draft public hearing notice and noted the estimated assessed tax rate would be updated to approximately $5.52 based on new assessment data. After brief discussion about the net impact on a $300,000 home (approximately $30 reduction in property taxes roughly offsetting the $30 garbage fee increase), the Finance Committee approved the notice with the amended tax rate. The full Board voted 5-2 to approve, with Trustees Clark and Beck voting nay. The public hearing is scheduled for the November 16th board meeting at 6 PM.

title: Public Health & Safety Committee Meeting
overview: The Wausau Public Health & Safety Committee voted unanimously to recommend striking the 2027-2028 Flock camera contract appropriations and directing the police to immediately cease using the surveillance cameras — a significant civil liberties decision driven by strong community opposition. The committee also received an impressive update on the city's Community Care Paramedic program, which has achieved a 63% reduction in 911 calls among enrolled patients, and discussed deer and feral cat management, a tavern shooting incident involving 100 demerit points, and the police department's third quarter report.

discussions.item: Flock Camera Contract — Cease Use and Strike Future Appropriations
discussions.body: Alder Solanski moved a two-part motion: refer to the Finance Committee to strike 2027 and 2028 Flock contract appropriations, and refer to the Common Council to direct the police department to immediately cease using Flock cameras and bag them so Flock cannot access them. Alder Trueblood expressed concern about breach of contract implications, noting the city's commitments should mean something. Alder Lukens voted in favor citing reports that Flock had reinstalled cameras in other municipalities after contracts were terminated. Alder Solanski explained the two-part structure addressed both financial liability and continued surveillance separately, noting the city had already spent $150,000 on the contract. A question arose about whether the Marathon County Sheriff's Department could still place Flock cameras on county roads within the city; city attorney indicated the county could place cameras on county property without city authorization. The motion passed unanimously.

discussions.item: Community Care Paramedic Program Update
discussions.body: Community Paramedic Matt Kozlowski (also referred to as Kosloski in self-introduction) presented an 8-minute condensed report on the program's first year and a half. The program has served approximately 50-70 patients and achieved a 63% reduction in 911 calls — 273 fewer calls — translating to an estimated $300,000 in avoided medical bills for vulnerable residents. Kozlowski shared case studies including an elderly veteran nearly evicted due to suspected dementia, a patient triple-dosing diabetes medication out of confusion, and an elderly woman repeatedly falling due to a broken sofa, all of whom received direct hands-on assistance. Alders Solanski and Lukens praised the program; Kozlowski noted he is currently the only community paramedic for Wausau and is working with Aspirus to expand to Stevens Point, Merrill, and Wisconsin Rapids.

discussions.item: Deer and Feral Cats Within City Limits
discussions.body: Alder Solanski raised the issue as her most frequently heard constituent complaint, noting uncertainty about what the city can actually do. Patrol Captain Melinda Pauls outlined existing options: archery hunting is permitted on private property and some city property with police department registration; the DNR has an online nuisance deer reporting portal; and the city could request additional deer tags from the DNR as Rib Mountain has done. On feral cats, Pauls noted three CSOs are still dedicated to animal control. The chair and Alder Solanski suggested publicizing existing ordinances against feeding wild animals through the city newspaper and improving the city website's usability for residents seeking quick animal-related guidance.

discussions.item: Police Department Third Quarter Report
discussions.body: Captain Pauls noted it was another busy quarter with a focus on mental health calls and high-risk calls. No specific figures were discussed in the meeting beyond what was included in the written packet. The committee had no questions and placed the report on file.

discussions.item: Tavern Activities Report — August and September / 100-Point Demerit Incident
discussions.body: Captain Pauls described an incident in which a gunshot victim arrived at Aspirus hospital and investigation traced the shooting to a Wausau bar. Surveillance video and witness statements — including one indicating a bartender announced shots fired to help patrons flee before police arrived — led to the establishment receiving 100 demerit points for failing to report the shooting. Alder Watson asked what demerit points mean; it was explained that at 100 points, the city sends a letter of concern and the establishment's owners are summoned to appear before the committee at the next meeting for the committee to determine penalties such as fines or license suspension. The committee confirmed the matter would appear on the next agenda. A 50-point violation at a venue called Intermission was noted but no action was taken, as the threshold for committee action is 100 points.

publicComment: No public comment was offered during the recorded portion of the meeting. However, Alder Solanski referenced strong community input received in preceding weeks opposing the Flock cameras, and the chair thanked the community for showing up to various meetings on the topic.

overview: The Wausau Police & Fire Commission held a brief meeting that included dismissal of a citizen complaint reconsideration, followed by presentations from police and fire department leadership on budget proposals, recruitment, and technology updates. Key topics included proposed 2027 budget cuts for both departments, an active police recruitment process targeting 8-10 new hires, fire department apprentice program updates, and an informational presentation on the Flock Safety automated license plate reader (ALPR) system ahead of a public health and safety committee meeting that evening.

discussions.item: Dismissal of citizen complaint reconsideration (JV)
discussions.body: The meeting opened with a motion to dismiss the reconsideration of a citizen complaint identified only as 'JV.' The motion was made and seconded without debate, and was approved by voice vote. No discussion of the complaint's substance was recorded.

discussions.item: Wausau Police Department 2027 Budget Overview
discussions.body: In Chief Barnes's absence, a deputy chief-level official presented the proposed 2027 police budget. Key changes include ending the All Cities Management contract for adult crossing guards (saving ~$40,000), cutting the CSO budget by 50% (~$45,000 savings), maintaining the humane society non-dog stray contract at $18,500, restructuring the SRO contract to seek 100% school-year coverage by the district (~$50,000 savings), and reducing authorized sworn staff from 81 to 80 as foundation funding for the downtown officer program phases out. The city council also approved a $50,000 feasibility study into the UW-Stevens Point campus as a potential future police and fire facility.

discussions.item: Police Recruitment Update
discussions.body: Captain Pauls reported that a recruitment process launched in August drew just over 40 applicants, down sharply from approximately 400 applicants 25 years ago, though the quality of candidates was described as strong. The department is hiring 8 to 10 officers to address current vacancies and four anticipated retirements in early 2025. Twelve background investigations are currently underway, with at least three candidates expected to be brought to the commission at a special November 5th PFC meeting, as some candidates are also considering other departments.

discussions.item: Flock Safety ALPR System Update
discussions.body: Captain Graham provided an update on the department's Flock Safety automated license plate reader program, which has been before committee or council approximately seven or eight times since a contract was signed in 2023. He illustrated the system's reactive and proactive capabilities with a retail theft case in which ALPR identified a suspect vehicle, linked it to over $5,000 in additional thefts, and enabled a traffic stop while the suspect was returning to commit another theft. A commission member raised privacy concerns about potential misuse by officers or third parties, particularly in domestic violence situations; Captain Graham explained that public access to the system is not possible, that officer access requires multi-factor authentication, and that the system is CJIS compliant with monthly and annual audits. A transparency portal on the department's website was noted. The chair reminded the commission that its jurisdiction is largely limited to hiring, discipline, and investigations, making the discussion informational in nature.

discussions.item: Fire Department 2027 Budget and Hiring Update
discussions.body: Fire Chief [name not stated in transcript] reported that proposed 2027 budget cuts are achieved primarily by leaving the Division Chief of Training position—vacant since January 2025—open until July 1, 2027, and leaving a second position in the inspection bureau open for six months following an upcoming retirement. On hiring, the department interviewed two candidates in closed session earlier that day and had three more interviews scheduled that afternoon, with an additional application received the prior Friday. Nine new firefighter apprentices began three weeks prior and are now on 48-hour shifts while attending NTC two to three days per week.

discussions.item: Fire Department Succession Planning
discussions.body: The fire chief described plans to present a revised organizational chart to HR and the finance department before year-end, aimed at building redundancy and succession pathways. A key element would formally integrate the community care paramedic position under the EMS Division Chief, given that roughly 80% of city calls are EMS-related and the division currently has limited leadership redundancy. The chief noted a Lieutenant promotion interview will also need to be scheduled, potentially requiring a special December PFC meeting.

discussions.body: Supervisor Robinson announced the HR Finance & Property Committee would meet October 20 before the County Board to discuss funding for the county highway facility resolution, a resolution declaring November as Project Greenlight Month for veterans, and a resolution opposing proposed US Census rule changes that could shift Wisconsin 'snowbird' residents to states like Florida and Arizona, potentially costing Wisconsin a congressional seat and federal funding.

discussions.body: Supervisor Lemmer raised concerns about the county's shift from substantively reviewing town ordinances to a purely procedural compliance check, worrying about 'rubber stamping.' Corporation Counsel explained the shift is intentional and designed to limit county liability, noting towns that opt out of county zoning are responsible for enforcing their own ordinances. He acknowledged the odd statutory requirement for county approval even when towns have opted out, and confirmed the Reedbrock ordinance had previously been returned to the town for a required new public hearing before being resubmitted. Supervisor Sandowski asked whether the Wausau data center ordinance addressed hyperscale data centers; Chair Gibbs reiterated the county's role is solely procedural compliance.

discussions.item: Cherokee Park land purchase — Resolution 66-26 (up to 15 acres, not to exceed $X)
discussions.body: Supervisor Jensen asked about the Knowles-Nelson Stewardship Fund referenced in the resolution; Administrator Landon and Supervisor Robinson explained the fund's legal framework exists but currently has no appropriation, and was included in case it is reauthorized so the county could capture outside funding. Supervisor Hagen asked three questions about need, tax impact, and maintenance costs; Parks Director Jamie Paully (participating remotely) explained the parcel is forested riverfront land that would make Cherokee Park 'whole' by eliminating a gap along the river, that taxable value lost would be minimal given current forest classification, and that no additional maintenance costs are anticipated unless trails or improvements are added in the future.

discussions.item: Phase four highway facility construction — educational presentation
discussions.body: Deputy Administrator and Facilities Director Chris Holman led an extensive presentation alongside project architect Ned Dirksen, Miron project executive Eric Brandt, and Excel Engineering's geothermal specialist Corey Powers. The guaranteed maximum price for direct construction was presented as $53.3 million, with a total project cost of $54,980,537 including contingencies, design fees, and owner FF&E. Key topics included value engineering steps already taken (consolidating hazardous storage, switching to energy wheel, reducing card-access doors), geothermal HVAC justification (bore field cost $1.9 million with 40% IRA tax credit reducing county cost to approximately $1.14 million; Dunn County comparison showing 33% less electricity and 84% fewer natural gas therms), coal dust mitigation via MERV 8 and MERV 14 dual filtration, and a construction timeline targeting spring 2027 site work start and August 2028 substantial completion. Supervisors asked numerous questions about geothermal reliability in extreme cold (backup gas boilers confirmed), filter maintenance costs (Dirksen pledged to provide costs by Tuesday), LEED certification (architect stated equivalent energy efficiency measures are incorporated without pursuing formal certification), truck traffic flow, building expansion capacity, and whether competitive bidding was followed (Holman confirmed sealed public bid process with lowest qualified bidder selection and validation calls completed by Miron).

discussions.item: Approval of Minutes - August 18 and September 15, 2026 APC Meetings
discussions.body: Trustee Solheim moved to approve both sets of minutes and Misty Swanson seconded. The motion passed 3-0 with all three members present voting in favor.

discussions.item: Comparative Internal Financial Statements Year to Date August 2026
discussions.body: Finance Director John reported a general fund budget surplus of $364,000 at the end of August versus $667,000 at the same point in 2025, with 57% of budget spent at 67% of the year elapsed. He flagged the village attorney, municipal building, and garbage/refuse/solid waste accounts as likely to exceed budget, with a budget amendment expected at the November board meeting. Trustee Fridell asked about the surplus and noted concern about whether expenditures are outpacing revenues due to insufficient net new construction, and expressed enthusiasm about the distribution center project as a financial turning point. John noted that excess TID 1 revenues can annually repay the $2.7-2.8 million village advance without waiting until 2044, and said details would be shared at the upcoming Monday-Tuesday budget workshops.

discussions.item: 2025-27 State Aids Listings for 2027 Budget
discussions.body: John reported a $56,000 increase in total state aids for 2027, driven primarily by a $52,000 increase in transportation aids attributable to capital spending on Kronenwetter Drive and the new public works garage. He noted that the aid formula has not yet captured 2026-2027 staffing increases, and anticipated the trend would continue upward as road miles grow with the Green Tree subdivision and FAA property development.

discussions.item: August 2026 Financial Satisfaction Report from Wisconsin Policy Forum
discussions.body: John presented charts comparing Kronenwetter to 10 North Central Wisconsin communities using 2024 data, showing the village near the bottom in general government spending per person ($120), street surface maintenance ($147 per person), police spending ($163 per person), net basic spending ($477), and net operating spending. He highlighted that 84% of the tax base is residential — the highest of all compared communities — contrasted with low per-person property taxes ($317). Trustee Fridell commented that the data supports the case for sound financial management and urged clear public communication of these facts to build resident credibility. The presentation was framed as context for the upcoming budget discussions.

discussions.item: Capital Improvement Program 2027-2036 Second Draft
discussions.body: Administrator Dave and John presented the second draft of the 10-year CIP, noting the parks committee had now added their numbers across the full plan period. For 2027, the plan totals approximately $4.3 million with only 43% as general obligation debt; the two borrowing items are Maple Ridge Road reconstruction and Bushka Park playground equipment. John noted $1.2 million in unspent 2024 borrowing proceeds available for the Maple Ridge project, which must be spent by October 2027. Discussion included a new Wisconsin residential TIF law effective October 1, 2026 that developers have already raised with the administrator as a possible infrastructure financing tool, with suggestions to engage the DOR or the village's financial advisor Ellers for guidance. Martin Road was discussed as a future high-cost full reconstruction project. Dave noted the CIP will be a separate board resolution from the budget.

discussions.item: Debt Service Fund Tax Levy Strategy
discussions.body: John explained that $863,200 in unused TID 2 borrowing proceeds will be transferred to the capital project fund, shifting the associated debt obligation from TID 2 to the village tax levy fund. This restructuring reduces the originally projected two drops in debt service payments (in 2029 and 2035) to a single drop around $200,000 in 2029. The move accelerates TID 2's closure timeline, which John said he would discuss further at the budget workshop with additional detail from Ellers.

discussions.item: Municipal Center Hours
discussions.body: Administrator Dave proposed closing the municipal center to walk-in foot traffic on Friday afternoons to allow administrative catch-up time, while continuing to answer phones. He noted this mirrors Marathon County, City of Wausau, and other area municipalities. Trustee Solheim moved to recommend to the village board that hours be changed to Monday-Thursday 7:30 a.m.-4:30 p.m. and Friday 7:30 a.m.-noon, with Friday afternoons as an administrative day. The motion was amended to specify Friday as an all-day administrative day after noon. The roll call vote was 4-0 (Fridell, Swanson, Solheim, Stowell all yes) to send the recommendation to the board.

discussions.item: Written Public Comment Procedure for Village Meetings
discussions.body: Administrator Dave introduced a revised policy for Gen O10 governing written public comment submitted to village meetings, including a Wednesday deadline for inclusion in packets. He noted board members had requested this formalized procedure. Guy Fridell moved and Misty Swanson seconded to recommend the revisions to the village board. The roll call vote was 4-0 to forward to the board.

discussions.item: Ordinance 14-16 Police and Fire Commission and Utilities Committee Dual Service
discussions.body: Administrator Dave recommended against changing Ordinance 14-16, which prohibits an individual from serving simultaneously on the Police and Fire Commission and the Utilities Committee. He said village staff, both chiefs, and village counsel all oppose the change, citing the importance of keeping the PFC free from political influence. Both chiefs expressed concern about political bias affecting public safety departments. The committee agreed that the ordinance encourages broader citizen participation and diversity on boards. Trustee Fridell moved to recommend to the board that no changes be made to Ordinance 14-16; Trustee Solheim seconded. The roll call vote was 4-0 to send that recommendation to the board.

discussions.item: 2027 Operating Budget Preview - Utility Funds and General Fund
discussions.body: John reported that neither the water nor sewer utility rates will need to increase for 2027. The Red Mountain Metro assessment rose from $460,000 to an estimated $540,000 for 2027, but delaying sewer utility borrowing until after July 1, 2027 means no new debt service kicks in until 2028, enabling a near-balanced sewer utility budget ($7,800 projected surplus). A new half-time utility crew position will be split 50/50 between water and sewer utilities. On the general fund, diesel fuel surcharges on garbage collection are running approximately $57,000 over budget for the remainder of 2026 (over $9,000 per month), driven by diesel at $6.35/gallon; the village will absorb the overrun rather than issue a supplemental bill to residents. The garbage rate for 2027 will increase approximately $39-40 on the annual tax bill; Dave and John agreed to draft a joint explanatory letter to accompany the tax bill. Dave noted police union insurance costs came in at a 14% increase and the village is exploring switching officers to TeamCare as a cost-saving alternative, with union reps expressing openness to the change. Budget workshops were set for Monday at 3 p.m. and Tuesday at 6 p.m., with printed budget binders to be distributed Friday.

title: City council Meeting
overview: The Wausau City Council held its first regular meeting in five weeks on October 13th, taking action on several significant items including approving full city funding for the private-side lead service line replacement program (estimated $4.5 million gap), passing a rezoning ordinance for Honey Locust Court over objections from the district alder, approving a transit fare collection system upgrade for Metroride, and defeating a drinking water treatment solar array project after EPA grant funding fell through. The meeting also featured extensive public comment on the Flock license plate reader camera system and boulevard snow plowing policy.

discussions.item: Proclamations
discussions.body: Mayor Diny presented three proclamations: one designating 2026 Fire Prevention Week with a focus on lithium-ion battery safety; one commending the Wausau Fire Department for rescuing two occupants — including a member of the U.S. House of Representatives — from a downed aircraft in Lake Wausau on September 12th; and one proclaiming October as Pedestrian Safety Month. Fire Chief Jeremy Cop accepted the rescue commendation on behalf of department personnel. Chris Filtz from the Bike and Pedestrian Advisory Committee accepted the pedestrian safety proclamation and highlighted committee accomplishments including the e-bike ordinance and faster sidewalk clearing requirements.

discussions.item: Public Comment on Flock License Plate Reader Cameras
discussions.body: Multiple speakers urged the council to terminate the city's contract with Flock Safety, a license plate reader camera vendor. Courtney Olsen and Felix Gallow, both of 1206 Highland Park Boulevard, asked the council to omit the $50,000 Flock payment from the 2027 budget, deliver written notice of termination under contract section 11.16, and pass a surveillance technology ordinance requiring a council vote before future acquisitions. Gallow cited a website at unflockwausau.org and alleged Flock improperly shares and monetizes resident data. Danielle Fischer echoed those concerns, stating studies showing crime reduction were funded by Flock or similar companies. No council action was taken on this issue at this meeting.

discussions.item: Public Comment on Boulevard Snow Plowing Policy
discussions.body: Five residents from Highland Park Boulevard and surrounding streets — Karen Briggs, Danielle Fischer, Carrie Mor, Alice Kether, and Mary Broadhead — thanked the Infrastructure Committee for passing a resolution (Resolution 5526) to permit counterflow plowing so that snow is directed to the median strip rather than to residents' driveways. Speakers asked the council to tighten the language of the resolution so it cannot be changed at departmental discretion, with Broadhead proposing specific amended wording directing that plowing on boulevard streets push snow to the median strip.

discussions.item: File 26-10003: Rezoning Honey Locust Court from SR2 to DR8
discussions.body: Alder Tierney (District 9) pulled this item and asked for postponement so residents could meet with the Planning Commission before a vote, arguing that placing eight twin-home structures per acre on the cul-de-sac represented a significant change for the Great Tree subdivision area. Director Feifer and city staff clarified that the adjacent 40 lots are already zoned DR8, the land is privately owned by the developer, and a public hearing had already been held. Alder Killian supported postponement, citing the importance of resident feedback. Alder Martins opposed postponement, arguing zoning would be consistent with the rest of Honey Locust Court. A motion to postpone to the next meeting (moved by Alder Neil, seconded by Killian) failed 3-8. The main motion to approve the rezoning then passed 8-3.

discussions.item: Youth Engagement Committee of the Whole
discussions.body: Alders Wiscowski and Terry Kilian brought forward a request to schedule a committee of the whole focused on youth engagement and retention in Wausau. Wiscowski outlined four objectives: directly engaging young people, gathering firsthand perspectives on leaving and staying in Wausau, workshopping ideas collaboratively, and identifying actionable endeavors for 2027. The format would involve student councils from Wausau East and Wausau West high schools in a relaxed workshop environment, with a follow-up session planned for April. Alder Lukans asked that the scope include youth who stay locally rather than only those who leave for college. The motion passed unanimously 11-0, with a tentative date in the first two weeks of December.

discussions.item: File 26-10005: Drinking Water Treatment Solar Array Project
discussions.body: Alder Martins explained that the Finance Committee had voted against the solar array project after the city failed to receive a U.S. EPA grant that would have covered up to 50% of costs. Without the grant, city borrowing would extend the payback period to nearly 20 years — close to the panels' expected 25-30 year lifespan. The Finance Committee voted to deny the project. The full council voted 0-11 against approving the project, effectively killing it.

discussions.item: File 26-10006: Funding Option for Private-Side Lead Service Line Replacement
discussions.body: Consultants from CIP presented data showing Wausau leads the nation in per-capita lead service line replacements, with over 3,500 lines replaced and approximately 2,850-2,900 remaining. Construction costs in Wisconsin have risen 56% over two years, and the current low-interest BIL (Bipartisan Infrastructure Law) funding at 0.25% is set to sunset. The Finance Committee recommended Option C — the city covers the full estimated $4.5 million private-side gap for 2027 rather than charging homeowners — on a 3-0 vote. Alder Martins explained the rationale was equity across all residents. The full council approved Option C unanimously 11-0.

discussions.item: File 26-0921: Lead and Galvanized Service Line Replacement Ordinance (Reconsidered)
discussions.body: The council first voted 9-2 to reconsider this ordinance, which had previously failed. Alder Hanniki proposed an amendment adding incremental repayment schedules (3-6 month or 1-2 year periods) for property owners responsible for remaining balances, but withdrew the amendment after the council passed full city funding under File 26-10006, making the repayment language largely moot. City Attorney Jacobson clarified that Section 9 of the ordinance regarding property owner responsibility is not inconsistent with the funding resolution but serves as a contingency for any stragglers after grant funding expires. Alder Wiscowski raised concerns about enforcement language (shall/may/will) and the penalty timeline. Staff indicated enforcement would focus on landlords who repeatedly refuse access. The ordinance was passed, though the final vote tally was not clearly stated in the transcript.

discussions.item: File 260905: WISGO/Cubic Fare Collection System for Metroride
discussions.body: Deputy Director Melinda presented on behalf of Metroride, explaining the new fare collection system allows payment via app, card, or traditional cash vault. Alder Killian confirmed cash payment remains an option for those without digital access. Alder Martins noted the system is largely grant-funded and also includes automated vehicle location (AVL) technology so riders can track bus arrival times. Alder True Blood raised access concerns, suggesting a vending machine at the transit depot be considered for future planning. The motion passed 11-0.

An additional speaker, Mary Broadhead (1101 Highland Park Blvd), spoke after the formal public comment period and proposed specific amended language for the snow plowing resolution directing plows to push snow toward the median strip.

title: Finance Committee Meeting
overview: The Wausau Finance Committee met on October 13, 2026, taking action on several budget and operational items including pet licensing fee changes, sale of America 250 banners, a lead hazard grant amendment, and a lead service line loan resolution. The meeting featured significant public comment opposing the city's Flock license plate reader camera system, and concluded with the committee scheduling a final 2027 budget workshop for October 20 at 6:30 p.m. to address outstanding amendments including liquor license fees, capital spending, and motor pool financing.

discussions.item: Public Comment – Flock Camera System
discussions.body: Three residents from the Highland Park Boulevard area spoke in opposition to the city's Flock automated license plate reader (ALPR) camera contract. Danielle Fischer argued the cameras are not a proven crime deterrent and raised concerns about facial recognition, cell phone geo-fencing, and data storage by Flock. Felix Gallo asked the committee to remove the $50,000 Flock appropriation from the 2027 budget, issue a written termination notice under section 11.16 of the agreement, and pass an ordinance requiring a public council vote before future surveillance technology acquisitions; he also alleged Police Chief Barnes had been misinformed about camera placement. Courtney Olson, identifying herself as a domestic violence agency director, cited documented misuse of Flock data to track victims and noted that the Wisconsin Institute for Law and Liberty is suing Waukesha County over warrantless Flock database searches; she asked for a written legal opinion from the city attorney on whether the December payment could still be stopped.

discussions.item: Item 3A: Dog and Cat License Fees
discussions.body: Alder Watson proposed adjusting the spayed/neutered dog or cat fee to $25 and the microchip discount to $10 for 2027, with any funding shortfall covered by reserves. Staff noted that puppies and kittens are currently licensed at a half-year rate, which can result in the city paying the county more than it collects, and suggested potentially eliminating the half-year puppy/kitten rate via ordinance amendment in the future. Watson's motion on the two fee changes was seconded by Alder Neil and approved by the committee.

discussions.item: Item 3B: Sale of America 250 Wausau Banners
discussions.body: Staff reported receiving calls from residents interested in purchasing the decorative banners used during the summer. The proposed prices were $25 for tapered banners and $35 for rectangular banners. Alder Watson moved to approve the sale at the prices recommended in the staff memo; the motion was seconded by Alder Tierney and approved unanimously.

discussions.item: Item 3C: Second Amendment to Marathon County Health Department Lead Hazard Reduction Grant Agreement
discussions.body: Staff presenter Tammy Strasser explained the amendment addresses audit findings requiring updated monitoring language, authorizes the county health department to purchase an XRF lead-testing machine using grant funds, and broadens the reimbursable positions to a catch-all category. She also noted the health department received a new $4 million state grant to expand lead abatement countywide. The motion was made by Alder Neil, seconded by Alder Hennekey, and approved.

discussions.item: Item 3D: Resolution to Reimburse Expenditures – Safe Drinking Water Revolving Loan Program (BIL SFY 27-28)
discussions.body: Staff explained this is a standard reimbursement resolution allowing the city to incur lead service line replacement costs before the loan closes, then get reimbursed. The city has requested approximately $18.16 million for 2027, though final allocations from the DNR could come in lower, which would reduce the scope of the program. Alder Henke asked about the risk of lower-than-expected reimbursement and was told the program would simply be scaled back. The motion was made by Alder Watson, seconded by Alder Neil, and approved.

discussions.item: Item 3E: Sole Source Request – Zoll Monitors and Ventilators for Fire Department
discussions.body: Fire Chief [name not stated] requested the item be postponed two weeks so the EMS Division Chief could present details. Alder Tyrrell raised concerns that the cardiac monitors appeared on the capital deferred projects list at $215,000 while simultaneously being brought forward as a sole source purchase, calling it 'disingenuous.' The chief explained the intent is to use Fire Assistance to Firefighters (FAT) money to save approximately $80,000 by acting before an April deadline, avoiding CIP funds. The committee agreed by consensus to table the item for two weeks.

discussions.item: Item 3F: Third Amendment – CIP Master Partnership Agreement (2027-28 Lead Service Line Replacement)
discussions.body: Staff explained this is an annual amendment to authorize Community Infrastructure Partners to continue professional services for the lead service line replacement program, now covering both 2027 and 2028 contingent on DNR funding. Alder Henke asked whether costs would scale with any reduction in project scope and was told yes. Alder Watson moved approval, seconded by Alder Henke, and the committee approved.

discussions.item: Item 4: August 2026 General Fund Financial Report Review
discussions.body: Finance staff reported that motor pool costs allocated to police, fire, and public works are expected to exceed budget and a budget amendment will be brought to the October 27th meeting. The refuse budget is also running over due to a diesel fuel escalator clause in the current contract. Revenue is tracking well, with licenses and permits strong, investment income exceeding budget despite slightly lower rates, and municipal court fee revenues expected to increase following a state adjustment raising court costs from $38 to $48 per citation in Q1 2026. No action was taken; the report was placed on file.

discussions.item: Item 3G: 2027 Budget – Discussion of Amendments and Fee Schedule
discussions.body: The committee discussed a spreadsheet of implemented and non-implemented 2% budget reduction measures. Members raised concerns that several of the four or five vacant positions counted as savings may not represent genuine permanent reductions — particularly the surveyor position (offset by contracted services), two fire positions (6-month deferrals only), and a third city attorney position. The chair emphasized the need to address long-term debt, noting that capital borrowing will significantly impact the 2028 levy, and called for a closer look at deferrable capital projects. Discussion of liquor and cigarette license fee increases was raised by Alder Tyrrell, with staff noting state statute caps and the need to benchmark against neighboring municipalities. The committee scheduled a final budget workshop for Tuesday, October 20, 2026 at 6:30 p.m.

title: Regular Meeting
overview: The Wausau School Board held its regular October 12, 2026 meeting, approving consent agenda items, voting to join a nationwide class action lawsuit against Meta, TikTok, Snap, and Google over social media harm to youth, approving the 2027-2028 school calendar with an early start date waiver already granted by DPI, and updating policy 2370 to recognize the Wisconsin Seal of Biliteracy. The board also received an update on Career and Technical Education programs including youth apprenticeships, and postponed a closed session superintendent evaluation to October 28 due to three board members being absent.

discussions.item: Consent Agenda Approval
discussions.body: The consent agenda was approved unanimously without discussion. It included staff appointments, replacements, contract changes, separations, leaves, retirements, minutes from four prior sessions (September 14, September 21 closed sessions, and September 28 special session), payment of bills, budget status, board member salaries, and donations from numerous community donors including Kulie Cards and Gaming, St. Andrew Lutheran Church, Walmart, and others.

discussions.item: Career and Technical Education and Work-Based Learning Update
discussions.body: CTE Coordinator John Winter presented an overview of CTE programs, recent community partnership events including a career day at Green Heck (60 students from East and West), the Build My Future event at Kobe Window with 400 students and 60 businesses, Food for America for fourth graders, and an Army Humvee visit to the auto shop. Winter detailed three work-based learning programs—Advanced Marketing Internship (48 students), Business Opportunities at West, and Youth Apprenticeship (72 students)—explaining the DWD grant structure, 450-hour requirement, and dual grant funding. Board members Charles Burger, Sarah Brock, and Cory Sillars asked questions about AI's impact on career clusters, the transition from 16 to 14 state career clusters, potential state budget funding for high school trades programs, and the possibility of county-wide or regional collaboration on CTE programs. Sillars raised the idea of inter-district collaboration to save costs, and Winter noted the aviation 101 WAVE program as an existing model.

discussions.item: Class Action Lawsuit Against Social Media Companies
discussions.body: Assistant Superintendent of Operations Dr. Elizabeth Channel presented details of a nationwide class action lawsuit against Meta, TikTok, Snap, and Google, alleging the companies designed platforms to addict youth, causing mental health harms including anxiety, depression, and suicidal ideation. Channel noted recent litigation victories including a $375 million New Mexico judgment against Meta and a $27 million settlement in a Kentucky school district case, and explained there is no upfront cost to the district—only a 25% contingency fee if damages are recovered. The board voted unanimously to approve a resolution authorizing retention of legal counsel and initiation of litigation. Board President Bouché read the full resolution aloud before the vote.

discussions.item: 2027-2028 School Calendar Approval
discussions.body: The board was informed that the DPI waiver for an early school start date—previously presented at the September Committee of the Whole by Communications Coordinator Diana White and Assistant Superintendent of Academics Dr. Katie Caswell—had been approved by DPI as of the prior week. The board voted unanimously to approve the 2027-2028 school calendar pending that waiver, which had already been granted to allow an early start due to anticipated construction.

discussions.item: Policy 2370 - Educational Opportunities (Wisconsin Seal of Biliteracy)
discussions.body: The board voted unanimously to approve proposed changes to Policy 2370, Educational Opportunities, to formally recognize the Wisconsin Seal of Biliteracy as an educational opportunity offered in the district. Dr. [Johnsky/Tossky - name unclear in transcript] had presented the background information at the September Committee of the Whole meeting. No additional discussion was noted at this meeting.

discussions.item: Board Member Professional Growth, Recognitions, and Closed Session Postponement
discussions.body: Board President Bouché recognized Sarah Brock for achieving WASB Level 2 status and acknowledged his own WASB Level 5 recognition, both awarded at the Region 5 WASB meeting. Sillars noted he would attend DPI boundary appeal board hearings on October 20-21 in Hortonville regarding a potential school district dissolution, which could reduce Wisconsin's 421 districts. Bouché announced the closed session for superintendent evaluation was postponed to October 28 because three board members were absent and he wanted all nine members present for the evaluation.

overview: The Village of Weston Plan Commission held its regular meeting on October 13, 2026, approving a conditional use permit for US Venture/US Auto Force to operate a tire cross-dock freight terminal at 6002 Industrial Drive, and approving an amended extension for Bug Properties LLC to complete site improvements at 6406 Scoffield Avenue by staggered deadlines. The commission also acknowledged site plan modifications for the Mountain Bay Metropolitan Police Department facility and authorized staff to issue an early start permit for footings and foundation pending setback verification.

discussions.item: Public Comment – General
discussions.body: One speaker (identified as Jim) delivered pointed criticism of the planning and zoning department's reactive rather than proactive approach to conditional use permit compliance, specifically questioning how a property owner was allowed to occupy a non-ADA-compliant, unsafe building for months without enforcement action. Jim questioned why there was no ongoing dialogue with applicants during the two-year permit window and stated, 'Does it take for someone to get killed in that building and then oh my goodness, now we'll do something.' A second online commenter, Jacob Beldock, confirmed his written email regarding US AM31/47 Grand Avenue CUP 2024-0072 had been included in the packet.

discussions.item: Item 5: US Venture Inc. – Conditional Use Permit for Freight Terminal at 6002 Industrial Drive
discussions.body: Planner Jennifer presented the request for a CUP for a cross-dock tire distribution operation with two inbound 53-foot semis per day, seven delivery box trucks, and no outdoor storage. Applicant representative James Fland (Director of Real Estate, US Venture/US Auto Force) participated online, explaining the operation relocates from Rib Mountain and employs seven people. A neighbor, Brian (305 [street name]), raised concerns about traffic safety on the recently rebuilt path along the street given e-bikes and scooters, as well as noise and hours of operation. Jim P. spoke in support, noting he had a 20-year relationship with the company and stating the commission was acting in a quasi-judicial role under Wisconsin's 'shall issue' standard for conditional use permits. A motion to approve including a stormwater/tracking condition initially failed for lack of a second; a revised motion was approved removing condition D (limiting on-site trailer staging) and adding a condition requiring the applicant to work with village staff on preventing gravel/dirt tracking onto the road. An amendment adding the tracking/stormwater condition was voted on separately and approved before the main motion passed.

discussions.item: Item 6: Bug Properties LLC – Amendment to CUP 2023-0129 at 6406 Scoffield Avenue
discussions.body: Staff planner Jennifer and code official Roman presented the noncompliance status of Bug Properties LLC, with approximately 30% of required concrete installed and multiple accessibility, signage, and permit issues outstanding nearly three years after original CUP approval. The applicant, Bruce Gus, was not present at the start of the hearing and joined Zoom late, after the public hearing had already been closed. Jim P. (public commenter) expressed frustration that the applicant was not present and questioned the department's lack of proactive communication. Commissioners debated whether to grant the requested one-year extension to September 30, 2027, with several members objecting to that timeline. The commission approved a staggered amendment: all items except concrete must be completed by November 30, 2026, with concrete work extended to September 30, 2027.

discussions.item: Item 7: Special Exception Sign Permit – Turf MD at 5605 Meer Street
discussions.body: Staff presented a request to replace the cabinet on an existing 20-foot freestanding pylon sign that has a 5-foot setback where current code requires a 20-foot setback equal to sign height. Staff noted the pylon was originally installed in 1996 under old standards. Commissioners agreed the sign could not practically be relocated and approved the special exception sign permit unanimously with minimal debate.

discussions.item: Item 8: Mountain Bay Metro Police Department Site Plan Modification – 3600 Community Center Drive
discussions.body: Police Chief and project representatives explained that a TC Energy gas pipeline was found to be located outside its recorded 1960s easement, forcing the building footprint to shift approximately 12 feet west and the parking lot to be reconfigured, including adding a pedestrian walkway to the front entrance. The commission acknowledged the site plan changes and voted to recommend the Village Board authorize staff to issue an early start permit for footings and foundation only, contingent on verification that setback requirements are met, with a full amended site plan to return for formal approval in November 2026. Commissioner Zeyghami raised concern about whether TC Energy could excavate the parking lot in the future, and a commissioner suggested consulting the village attorney to explore whether TC Energy bears any cost obligations given the mislocated pipeline.

discussions.item: Item 11: Monthly Project Update – Tommy's Express and US AM31
discussions.body: Jennifer reported that Tommy's Express car wash had allowed its certificate of environmental insurance to lapse, with a new certificate in progress through corporate. Commissioners expressed serious concern about operating in a wellhead protection area without insurance coverage. One commissioner recommended that future conditional use permits include an automatic termination provision if the certificate of insurance expires, with a 30-day advance notification requirement, arguing staff should not have to bring this to the commission — it should be an automatic enforcement mechanism.

overview: The Village of Weston Public Works Committee met on October 12, 2026, covering a range of infrastructure and utility topics including ongoing road construction projects, a proposed pedestrian crossing on Business 51, sewer rate options for 2027, and an infiltration/inflow study. The committee approved several engineering contracts and directed staff to develop additional sewer rate scenarios for a future decision, with a goal of reaching at least a break-even position.

discussions.item: Sidewalk Snow Plowing Policy
discussions.body: Staff noted receipt of an email from a resident whose side yard abuts Fuller Street regarding sidewalk snow plowing. Staff explained the village generally does not plow residential sidewalks except where there is no boulevard and snow is plowed directly onto the sidewalk. A committee member requested it be placed on next month's agenda for discussion, and staff agreed.

discussions.item: CIP/DIP Project Update
discussions.body: Staff reported Western Avenue is substantially complete with warranty concrete work ongoing; contractor Treeweiler requested that some larger concrete panel replacements be deferred to spring to avoid fresh concrete being damaged by road salt, which staff said would remain under warranty at no extra cost. Committee members debated the cause of widespread concrete spalling in central Wisconsin, noting it is not isolated to Weston. Bladel Avenue and Concord at Bayberry Street were described as nearing asphalt paving. Well Four is complete, Well Three rehabilitation is ongoing with an April go-live target. The Military Road project is finished. Granite Ridge subdivision has four homes under construction.

discussions.item: Fleet and Street Operations Report
discussions.body: Street operations staff reported stockpiling over 52,000 yards of sand from ongoing projects for future road subgrade improvements in areas like Howland Avenue and Woodland Drive. A committee member raised a question about respiratory PPE for the employee spray-painting crosswalks and requested staff check the SDS for the latex-based paint given it is being spray-applied. Staff agreed to follow up on that safety question.

discussions.item: Business 51 Sidewalk Crossing at Newport
discussions.body: Staff reported following up with the DOT after last month's meeting. The DOT indicated their preliminary safety evaluation found no documented pedestrian impacts (no one hit), which did not meet their threshold for warranted crossing funds. Staff and committee members argued that pedestrians are observed walking in the median to reach signalized intersections, which is unsafe even if no collision has occurred. The DOT indicated they need the village to formally indicate interest in the crossing before refining cost estimates; current figures of $20,000 for road widening and $10,000–$30,000 for behind-sidewalk grading were described as very preliminary. A committee member moved to proceed with pursuing the crossing including flashing beacons and to also refer the matter to the Public Safety Committee; the motion passed unanimously.

discussions.item: Proclamation 2026-002: Crash Responder Safety Week
discussions.body: Staff explained the Wisconsin DOT's Traffic Incident Management Enhancement program requested municipalities issue a proclamation for Crash Responder Safety Week (November 2–6, 2026) to raise awareness about slowing down and moving over for crash responders. The committee moved to recommend approval of the proclamation, which passed unanimously.

discussions.item: 2027 Sanitary Sewer Rate Options
discussions.body: Staff presented six rate scenarios to address a 2025 operating loss of approximately $440,000 and a projected $100,000 increase in Rim Mountain Metro costs for 2027. Options ranged from doing nothing to recovering losses over two or three years or matching neighboring community rates. Committee members discussed the trade-offs between rate shock and gradual increases, whether to establish a tiered industrial rate, and whether INI study results reducing inflow could affect future costs. No rate was set; the committee directed staff to bring back additional scenarios (described informally as options G and H between scenarios E and F), historical Weston cost trend data, and Rim Mountain Metro multi-year billing history for further discussion next month, with a goal of implementing a new rate by January.

discussions.item: Sanitary Sewer INI Study Results
discussions.body: Staff presented a preliminary excerpt from Inpipe Technologies' infiltration and inflow study covering the sewer system in the Rothschild boundary area (Alderson/Weston Ave to Vulkman, west to Highway 29). Staff explained the study uses flow trackers to distinguish groundwater infiltration from rain-driven inflow and can prioritize problem pipe reaches. Staff identified basins 3.0 and 2.0 near Highway 29 and Alderson as areas of concern not yet addressed. The committee acknowledged the report and directed staff to invite Inpipe Technologies to present the full study results at the next meeting, with 20 minutes allocated.

discussions.item: Potential Utility Easement: Executive Court to Kramer Lane
discussions.body: Staff described an opportunity to secure a utility easement as a private property owner at 7209 Executive Court purchases a strip of land from a neighbor to the north, which would enable future water main looping out to Kramer Lane. Without the loop, the entire Edgewood Estates subdivision relies on a single connection at North Apache and Edgewood. The committee agreed it was worth pursuing and voted to direct staff to analyze potential easement costs and return with findings at a future meeting.

discussions.item: Engineering Design Contract: Vulkman Street, Business 51 to McIntyre
discussions.body: Staff presented a revised quote from Becker Hoppy for $22,500 to design water main infrastructure on Vulkman Street from Business 51 to McIntyre, matching Rothschild's shared cost for their half of a water main redundancy project. Staff recommended pausing the McIntyre portion pending clarity on the junior high school's future. The committee approved the $22,500 contract.

discussions.item: Business 51 Storm Pond Construction Services Contract
discussions.body: Staff presented Strand Associates' proposal of $92,800 for construction oversight and clean water fund loan administration for the Business 51 storm pond project, with Weston's share at $65,424 and the remainder split with Rothschild and Scoffield. Staff noted the DOT has not yet confirmed participation. A committee member suggested making approval contingent on partner community approval; the motion passed as amended with that contingency.

discussions.item: 2027 Street Maintenance Plan
discussions.body: Staff presented a draft plan totaling approximately 2.36 miles of asphalt overlay and just under 4.5 miles of GSB sealant, plus concrete repairs on Scoffield Avenue (westbound lanes), repaving of East Everest Avenue (rated 2 on PASER scale) near the new Mountain Bay Metro Police Department entrance, and a portion of Woodland Drive. Total budget is $850,000 across operating and CIP funds. Staff noted the plan hits the budget limit and the goal is to get bids out over winter to avoid spring scrambles. The committee approved the plan as presented.

overview: The Wausau Human Resources Committee met on October 12th and took action on two items: approving a request for an additional HR staff member (to be incorporated into the 2027 budget rather than a budget modification), and voting to maintain the existing summer hours schedule and traditional full-week winter hours rather than adopting year-round summer hours. The HR staffing approval is significant as a previous attempt to add the position had failed at common council.

discussions.body: Alder Wowski moved to approve the minutes from preceding meetings and Alder Larson seconded. The motion passed on a voice vote with no opposition.

discussions.item: Reintroduction of Request to Approve Additional HR Department Staff Member
discussions.body: The acting HR director presented a detailed case for an additional HR coordinator, citing 24 active workers' compensation cases, complex FMLA administration, and an overall unsustainable workload. Alder Killian expressed full support, saying the workload 'looks unsustainable.' Alder Martins moved for approval, seconded by Alder Buscowski, and the motion passed. Discussion followed about timing: a prior budget modification had already been approved by finance and sent to common council but did not pass, so the committee agreed the position would instead be built into the 2027 budget, with posting anticipated on or after January 2nd.

discussions.item: Recommendation to Establish Summer Hours as Year-Round City Hall Schedule
discussions.body: HR staff proposed making summer hours (Monday–Thursday 7:15 a.m.–4:30 p.m., half-day Friday) permanent year-round, noting that extended Tuesday evening hours attracted only five visitors all summer, three of whom came between 5:00 and 6:00 p.m. Alder Killian opposed year-round summer hours, arguing the city has a responsibility to be open during standard business hours including Friday afternoons, and moved to keep summer hours in summer while restoring full business hours in winter with one extended evening; that motion received no second. Alder Martins raised concern about closing Friday afternoons in winter and suggested a pilot for evening hours. Alder Larson moved to keep summer hours as summer hours and restore traditional full five-day winter hours, seconded by Alder Martins; that motion passed on a voice vote.

discussions.item: Winter Street Maintenance Policy — Counterflow Plowing on Center Median Boulevard Streets
discussions.body: After extensive public comment from roughly ten speakers over several months of meetings, Alder Slonsky moved to amend the Department of Public Works winter maintenance policy to permit snowplow counterflow to traffic whenever otherwise safe to do so; the motion passed unanimously. City Attorney Ann Jacobson confirmed Wisconsin Statute 346.05(2) allows vehicles engaged in highway maintenance to operate on the left-hand side of the road, and that a written internal policy would protect plow drivers under city liability. DPW Director Dustin [last name inaudible] acknowledged the counterflow practice had been discontinued based on a misinterpretation — originally prompted by a state patrol comment about one-way streets that was incorrectly applied to divided two-way boulevard streets. Alder Slonsky criticized DPW for not providing requested cost/time comparisons between plowing methods as asked at the prior meeting, while Alder Martins and others praised community advocates for their thorough, data-driven advocacy over three years. District 1 Alder Carol Lukans appeared as a public commenter urging the committee to act that night so residents would not face another winter under the old policy.

discussions.item: Assessment Rates for 2027 Construction Projects
discussions.body: City engineering staff presented proposed 2027 assessment rates, noting that at $55 per accessible foot the city recovers roughly 22% of roadway reconstruction costs — down from a historical target of 60%. Staff recommended raising the sewer lateral replacement assessment from $500 (unchanged for approximately 25 years) to $1,000, noting actual city costs range from $1,500 to $2,500 per lateral. Alder Martins moved to approve the rates with street reconstruction raised to $60 per accessible foot and the sewer lateral assessment raised to $1,000; the motion passed unanimously. Alders Heni and Slonsky raised questions about whether percentage-based assessments would be fairer than flat dollar rates, but staff explained that flat rates are required for statutory notice purposes and provide more equity across projects of varying complexity.

discussions.body: A motion was made and seconded to vacate the alley; city engineering noted a sanitary sewer runs through the alley and the city must retain an easement. A friendly amendment was adopted to include easement retention language, and the motion passed unanimously. Public commenter Michael Moran (2513 Elmwood Boulevard) spoke in support of the vacation during public comment.

discussions.body: A speaker at the public hearing representing property owners Chris and Margaret [Gdori, phonetic] testified in support, explaining the owners want to secure the end of the road as a private drive. City engineering confirmed both sewer and water infrastructure are present and easements must be retained. Alder Heni moved to vacate with easement language; Alder Slonsky seconded after confirming engineering had no objection. A committee member asked for clarification that the remainder of Liberty Ridge Way remains a public road, which staff confirmed. The motion passed unanimously.

discussions.item: Painted Curb Extension Project — Fourth Street and Scott Street (Wausau River District)
discussions.body: TJ [last name not stated] from city staff presented a River District proposal to install plastic bollards and road paint at the east side of the Fourth and Scott intersection downtown to create pedestrian refuge areas and shorten crossing distances. The project had already been approved by the Bike and Pedestrian Committee. The River District committed in writing to cover bollard replacement costs through 2032; the Center for Visual Arts provided verbal assurance of low- or no-cost repainting assistance. Alder Slonsky moved to approve; Alder Martins seconded and expressed strong support, noting it was a proven traffic-calming method at a difficult intersection. The motion passed unanimously. Alder Wizkowski suggested exploring additional painted intersection treatments downtown, with staff noting that could be brought to a joint Bike Ped and Arts Commission meeting.

discussions.item: 2027-2028 Capital Infrastructure Projects Review
discussions.body: Alder Heni raised concerns about the sustainability of current borrowing levels, noting the levy is rising again, and said he is working with Director Linman to identify capital projects that could be deferred to reduce borrowing by $4–5 million. Alder Martins noted that the drinking water treatment facility solar array (projected at $1.98 million) effectively failed after a U.S. EPA grant was not received, and that a downtown street traffic flow redesign at $150,000 is still under discussion tied to TID 12. Staff emphasized that deferring road reconstruction has ripple effects pushing all subsequent projects back and frustrating residents expecting scheduled work.

discussions.item: 2026 Construction Projects Update
discussions.body: Staff reported that the downtown utility project (Second Street and Division Street), Grant Street utility upgrades, and Stark Street reconstruction (5th to 12th) are all 100% complete. Eighth Avenue reconstruction (Bridge to Spruce) is approximately 90% complete with final paving expected the week of October 19th. Asphalt overlays and sidewalk projects are complete city-wide. The riverfront parking lot near Athletic Park is under construction with paving expected the following week. Staff noted this is one of the earliest project completion years in recent memory. Discussion touched on coordination challenges with the lead service line replacement contractor, and committee members advocated for better public-facing communication tools — including a simpler website flowchart and use of the existing pothole hotline (715-261-6960) and Wausau Streets email — to reduce resident confusion about road work timelines.

title: Finance Committee Budget Session #3
overview: The Wausau Finance Committee held its third budget session for the 2027 budget, covering special revenue funds, capital projects, TID districts, debt service, and enterprise funds. A significant portion of the meeting focused on the city's growing debt burden, with Alderperson Hani presenting eight budget proposals including capping borrowing, finding $4.2-5.2 million in deferrable capital projects, cutting the city administrator position, and requesting a 1% general fund reduction. The committee agreed not to meet Thursday as planned, instead giving time for members to submit written amendments for a future meeting.

Public comment on agenda items
