discussions.item: Special Revenue Funds Overview
discussions.body: Finance Director Maryanne presented the special revenue funds including community development block grant, economic development, environmental cleanup, room tax, recycling, animal control, hazmat, and the 400 Block Riverlife fund. She noted the environmental cleanup fund reserves are declining now that an insurance annuity from the Holtz Kroy settlement has ended, and costs from EPA oversight — including a $121,000 bill last year — will eventually return to the levy. She also suggested consolidating some special revenue funds into the general fund to build up the expenditure restraint base, noting the city receives over $1 million in expenditure restraint grant funding.

discussions.item: Capital Projects Discussion
discussions.body: Engineering staff walked through 2027 infrastructure projects including Ethel Street reconstruction, 11th Avenue, 17th Avenue STP Urban design, asphalt overlay (proposed increase from $600,000 to $800,000), lead service line replacement, and sidewalk repair. Alderperson Hani raised concern about borrowing for basic infrastructure and asked whether projects like Ethel Street could be deferred to 2028; engineering staff explained deferral simply shifts the entire street reconstruction schedule back a year and increases ongoing maintenance costs. A committee member questioned why the city pays for alley paving excavation costs while residents are assessed only for asphalt, prompting discussion about revisiting that policy.

discussions.item: TID Districts Review
discussions.body: Economic Development Manager Patrick presented TID 8 (MBX South demolition and environmental cleanup, with a $250,000 WEDC brownfield grant applied for), TID 11 (business campus site prep and marketing for a large development site off Innovation Way), and TID 12 (limited expenditures due to ongoing deficits, projected to remain in deficit for approximately 10 years). Jefferson parking ramp HVAC replacement was identified as a critical project after one of two redundant systems failed. The former Sears ramp east wall — exposed after the Sears building demolition — needs $700,000 in waterproofing and rehabilitation. A Forest Street engineering and planning project of $150,000 was discussed as enabling future LRIP and STP Urban grant applications.

discussions.item: Debt Service Analysis
discussions.body: Maryanne presented a detailed debt analysis showing the city's outstanding general obligation debt at approximately 33.38% of equalized value (limit is 5%), projected to rise to 33.81% after proposed 2027 borrowing. She compared the 2016 infrastructure borrowing of $2.8 million at 1.54% interest (resulting in a $338,000 annual payment) to the proposed 2027 borrowing of $6.2 million estimated at approximately 4.27% (resulting in roughly $770,000 annually plus $216,000 for the lead service line loan). She proposed using TID 8's approximately $11 million in remaining increment capacity to absorb roughly $2.18 million in infrastructure costs, reducing the levy impact by approximately $275,000 annually. She also suggested a 10-year plan to incrementally add $130,000 per year to levy-funded capital to eventually take asphalt overlay and concrete repairs off debt.

discussions.item: Enterprise Funds: Metro Ride, Airport, Parking
discussions.body: The committee discussed that Metro Ride and the municipal airport operate at deficits covered by the general fund. Alderperson Hani raised constituent concerns about deficit operations, while Alderperson Tierney noted some municipal services like transit are inherently not self-sustaining but enhance quality of life. It was explained that Metro Ride cannot expand service to surrounding municipalities like Rib Mountain because those communities have not invited the city in and would need to help subsidize service, as Wisconsin does not permit regional transit authorities. New Metro Ride buses are coming through the Volkswagen emissions settlement. Airport revenue discussion included land lease payments, property taxes on privately-owned hangars, and past fuel-flow surcharge revenue that was discontinued when aviation fuel prices rose.

discussions.item: Storm Water Utility Discussion
discussions.body: Engineering Director Eric provided an overview of a storm water utility concept at committee request, explaining that currently 65% of storm water costs are borne by residential taxpayers rather than major impervious-surface users such as large parking lots and commercial buildings. A storm water utility would distribute costs based on equivalent dwelling units tied to impervious surface area, bringing in non-taxable entities like nonprofits as payers, with a corresponding reduction in the levy. Maryanne noted a consultant study funded by a grant is completed and a presentation is scheduled for the October 27th city council meeting.

discussions.item: Alderperson Hani's Budget Proposals and Next Steps
discussions.body: Alderperson Hani presented eight budget proposals including: capping 2027 borrowing at $17-18 million or reducing debt by $1 million; identifying $4.2-5.2 million in deferrable capital projects; a 1% general fund spending reduction; removing $150,000 for the city administrator position; a motorpool charge reconciliation; a current accounting of committed versus unassigned general fund balance; asking the mayor to direct Metro Ride, airport, and parking to develop 5-year financial plans; a reconciled capital project schedule; and a 5-year debt forecast separated by general government, water, and wastewater. The committee agreed not to meet Thursday, directing members to submit written amendments to Maryanne, who will distribute them and incorporate approved changes as a budget insert. Alder Watson was noted as also having proposals to submit.

discussions.item: Public Comment - Resident Water Quality Complaint
discussions.body: Resident Lori Foundry of Rainbow Drive/County Road XX described severe black and orange sludge in her water supply, corroded fixtures, clogged drains, and water she considers unsafe to drink or use for washing food. Greg (Public Works Director) explained the problem stems from manganese buildup at a dead-end line serving only two customers, and that flushing every six to eight weeks has not resolved the issue. The committee discussed options including pipe scrubbing, installing an RO filtration system, exploring a pipe-looping project estimated at $300,000–$400,000, and potentially obtaining an easement from a neighboring property. Staff committed to having lead water utility worker Mark Mackey visit the property to take water samples, and the committee expressed willingness to provide some form of bill compensation. The looping project was identified as a candidate for the Capital Improvement Plan.

discussions.body: Greg reported that wipes are clogging the vacuum-style Lift Station No. 3 nearly every day, requiring staff to spend roughly 1.5 hours daily clearing pumps at significant cost. The committee discussed using sewer cameras to identify offending addresses once a new utility employee starts the following Monday, and confirmed the village ordinance allows billing customers for damages caused by illegal dumping. discussions.body: Greg reported that the public works crew completed site excavation and gravel base work for the village garage project, and that ST Ellenbecker is expected to begin pouring concrete imminently, before cold weather requires heat blankets.

discussions.body: John (Finance/Treasurer) reported that the water utility showed revenues of approximately $513,000 through eight months against a positive fund balance of $183,000 after expenses, slightly below the prior year's $217,000 surplus. The sewer utility showed revenues of $786,000 against a surplus of $198,000, lower than the prior year's $312,000 due to elevated Rib Mountain Metro Sewage District charges that surged from a budgeted $460,000 to an estimated $572,000 for 2026. Total water utility debt stands at approximately $2.949 million, scheduled for payoff in 2043; the sewer utility currently carries no debt. No rate increases are anticipated for 2027.

discussions.item: Septic Tank Ordinance Discussion - Northland Lutheran High School Holding Tank Request
discussions.body: A representative from Northland Lutheran High School presented the school's request to install a holding tank for a small concession stand with two single-stall bathrooms used seasonally for soccer and baseball games, located approximately 407 feet from the nearest utility lateral. The committee developed amended ordinance language including: non-residential use only, seasonal use up to seven months, minimum 400 feet from nearest lateral, minimum lot size of one acre, tank size meeting Marathon County minimum requirements, and requiring approval from both the Public Works Director and the Utility Committee. Jim Buck moved and Dan Raskowski seconded to recommend the amended ordinance change to the Plan Commission and Village Board; the motion carried 4-0. Staff will draft language and consult the village attorney on whether a public hearing is required.

discussions.item: 2027 Budget Discussion - Water and Sewer Utilities
discussions.body: John and Greg presented the proposed 2027 utility budgets. No water or sewer rate increases are proposed for 2027. On the sewer side, projected revenues of approximately $1.371 million and inclusion of $548,100 in Rib Mountain Metro costs still yield a projected net profit of roughly $7,800, making a rate increase unnecessary. On the water side, revenues are projected at $947,000 driven in part by an estimated $90,000 in connection fees from the Marathon County garage project; after accounting for expenses including one additional half-time crew employee shared between water and sewer, the water utility is near break-even. The committee also discussed the Marathon County garage's plans to use wells for brine-making and car wash operations rather than municipal water, with committee member Alex Fedbeck pushing for a cost-benefit analysis on requiring municipal water connection to capture long-term revenue. Borrowing for the 2027–2029 CIP is proposed to be delayed until after July 1, 2027, to defer principal and interest costs to the 2028 budget.

title: Finance Committee Budget Session #2
overview: The Wausau Finance Committee held its second budget session for the 2027 budget, hearing presentations from the police, fire, transit, and general government departments. The session was dominated by a lengthy debate over Flock automated license plate recognition cameras, with several alderpersons expressing concern about civil liberties and data privacy while Police Chief defended the technology and its contractual obligations through 2028. No formal votes were taken during this session; budget amendments were held for later consolidation.

discussions.item: Police Department 2027 Budget
discussions.body: Police Chief presented a largely cost-to-continue budget with targeted savings totaling approximately $150,000, including: eliminating the contract with All City Management Services for crossing guards (saving ~$40,000–$45,000), cutting the CSO budget by roughly half (~$45,000), reducing the non-dog animal control (cat contract) budget from $37,000 to $18,500, and pursuing a renegotiated school resource officer contract with the school district at 100% district-funded cost for the school year (projected new revenue of $56,000). The department will also reduce sworn positions from 81 to 80 following expiration of Jed Alexander Foundation funding for downtown beat officers, while repurposing a patrol officer to continue the two-officer downtown program.

discussions.item: Flock ALPR Camera Debate
discussions.body: Alder Tom Neil called for removing the $50,000 Flock camera line item from the budget, citing concerns about corporate data practices and residents' distrust of the company. Alder Hani echoed concerns about Fourth Amendment implications and the potential for abuse of dragnet surveillance, though both alderpersons stated they trusted the current department leadership. The Police Chief defended Flock vigorously, stating the city's contract runs through December 31, 2028 with no exit-for-convenience clause, that data is city-owned and cannot be sold to third parties, that images are deleted after 30 days, and that exiting the contract could expose the city to financial liability. Mayor Doug Diny supported keeping the cameras, noting Wausau's policy is among the best in the state. Alder Tierney requested the department's written Flock policy be shared with all council members. The Police Chief noted a second public presentation to the Public Health and Safety Committee is scheduled for October 19th.

discussions.item: Animal Control Fee Amendment
discussions.body: Alder Watson proposed a budget amendment to reduce the 2027 pet license fee for spayed/neutered dogs or cats to $25 (from $30), with a $10 microchip discount, and fund any resulting revenue shortfall from the animal control fund balance of approximately $146,000. Finance Director Maryanne clarified that the fund balance is separate from approximately $41,954 held in a liability account owed to the county. Watson expressed intent to use the coming year to gather data on the program and have a deeper policy discussion about whether animal control should be partially levy-supported rather than fully user-fee funded. The amendment was tabled for later consolidation with other budget amendments.

discussions.item: Fire Department 2027 Budget
discussions.body: Fire Deputy Chief presented a budget relying on modest cuts across multiple line items — including eliminating the FDIC national conference travel, cutting psychological services, reducing software subscriptions, and proposing to purchase a robotic mower (~$10,000 savings) to eliminate the mowing contract at Station 2. The operations division chief position will remain vacant through July 1, 2027, and a retiring 40-hour employee's position will also be left open for six months to meet budget targets. The Chief noted the department is currently down six members from full staff and that overtime is a growing concern. A presentation on making the community care paramedic position permanent is forthcoming to the HR and Finance committees, with Aspirus verbally committing to continue funding support after the three-year trial ends in 2027.

discussions.item: Transit (Metro Ride) 2027 Budget
discussions.body: Transit Director Ron (approximately six months in the role) presented a budget reduced by $81,635 through historical spending analysis and adjustments. Key drivers of savings include 10 new buses replacing 2009-era vehicles, which will dramatically reduce fuel and maintenance costs as most of the fleet will be under warranty. The CAD AVL system cost increase will be fully covered by FTA ARPA funds through 2028, but will create a significant budget increase after 2029. A forthcoming UMO Wisco fare payment system, not yet before the council, would add operating costs but is projected to increase ridership. The FTA's indirect cost reimbursement rate increased from 10% to 15%, generating roughly $500,000 in general fund revenue that offsets the transit levy.

discussions.item: General Government Departments 2027 Budget
discussions.body: The city attorney's office and other general government departments presented small budgets with limited flexibility, primarily consisting of personnel, dues, licensing fees, and court-related costs. One assistant position in the city attorney's office remains frozen and unfilled. The office noted it recently left Westlaw, its online legal subscription service, as a cost-saving measure. Specific dollar amounts for general government savings were not detailed in the portion of the transcript captured.

overview: The Wausau City Council Economic Development Committee met on October 6th and took action on several items including directing staff to draft a deed restriction for 1300 Cleveland Avenue to prevent industrial use, approving a planning and due diligence agreement for the UWSP at Wausau campus, and approving a Habitat for Humanity development proposal at 424 Burns Street. The meeting concluded with the committee voting to adjourn into closed session to negotiate a potential city purchase of 108 Myron Street.

discussions.item: November Meeting Reschedule
discussions.body: Staff recommended moving the November 3rd meeting (Election Day) to Wednesday, November 4th, as Monday and Thursday were booked with other committees. The chair noted it would not work for Alder Tierney and that absent member Alder Lucans needed to be consulted. No formal motion was taken; staff was directed to confirm availability with Alder Lucans before finalizing the date.

discussions.item: 4A: 1300 Cleveland Avenue - EPA Technical Assistance and Deed Restriction
discussions.body: Staff reported the city has been confirmed eligible for EPA technical assistance, which would provide a consultant to conduct a financial feasibility analysis of reuse options identified through public engagement. Alder Kilian expressed concern that an email sent to the EPA by city staff characterized the public-identified reuse options as 'too narrow,' saying the committee and residents had never been told that. Kilian also raised that the property continues to be used for industrial purposes—including storage of trailers, old lampposts, and vehicles by DPW and the fire department—which she said undermined resident trust. City Attorney Jacobson confirmed it is legally permissible to place a deed restriction on city-owned property but noted the zoning has already been changed to residential and that any future council could remove a deed restriction. The committee debated how specific the restriction should be, with Alder Neil cautioning against language so narrow it might deter beneficial development. The committee ultimately directed staff and the city attorney, with input from Alder Kilian, to draft a deed restriction prohibiting industrial use consistent with public input meeting outcomes, to be brought back for formal approval at the next meeting. Staff also noted a 2024 council resolution allows limited DPW training use of the site, which may need to be revisited.

discussions.item: 4B: UWSP at Wausau Campus - Planning and Due Diligence Agreement
discussions.body: Director Fick explained the planning and due diligence agreement would give the city exclusive access to the county-owned UWSP campus property for six months to conduct architectural, engineering, and environmental review, contingent on a budget modification for the fire and police departments also passing at the next council meeting. Alder Neil noted a prior council vote on feasibility funding had failed but that the item was reintroduced after the required 30-day waiting period and would come before council the following Tuesday. The chair asked about Wausau School District interest in joint use; staff confirmed Chief Barnes has been meeting with the school district and they have expressed interest in partnering to share space and defray costs. Alder Killian moved to approve and the motion carried.

discussions.item: 4C: 424 Burns Street - Habitat for Humanity Proposal
discussions.body: Staff presented a Habitat for Humanity offer to purchase city-owned property at 424 Burns Street for approximately $12,000, with the plan to subdivide the parcel, sell a portion to an adjoining property owner, and build a Habitat home on the remainder. Alder Neil noted a strong track record with Habitat as a development partner and saw no need for closed session. He moved to approve the application, which was seconded by Alder Tierney and passed unanimously.

discussions.item: 108 Myron Street - Closed Session for Purchase Negotiations
discussions.body: Staff recommended entering closed session to discuss the potential city purchase of 108 Myron Street, citing that open discussion would compromise the city's negotiating position. Alder Neil made a formal motion citing Wisconsin Statute 19.85(1)(e) for deliberating on the purchase of public property for competitive or bargaining reasons. The motion passed on a voice roll call vote and the committee adjourned to closed session.

overview: The Marathon County Public Safety Committee met to discuss the ongoing Rib Mountain Law Enforcement Services contract negotiations, receive a 2027 budget overview for departments under committee jurisdiction, and address procedural disputes over meeting minutes. discussions.body: A supervisor (identified as Lance or Joel in context) disputed whether prior requests to add drones and flock cameras to the agenda had been recorded in committee minutes. Corporate counsel advised that minutes could only be amended to reflect requests made during the specific meeting in question, and that reconsidering already-approved minutes would require a formal motion for reconsideration. The committee agreed by consensus to defer approval of the current minutes pending chair review of video from the previous meeting to verify accuracy.

discussions.item: Rib Mountain Law Enforcement Services Contract Update
discussions.body: County Administrator Leonard reported that negotiations with Rib Mountain are ongoing and productive, with a follow-up meeting scheduled the following week involving the sheriff and Rib Mountain representatives. The current draft contract contemplates a fourth deputy in April of the following year, a fifth to be considered based on data review, and a goal of a 90/10 split for call response — meaning 90% of Rib Mountain calls answered by Rib Mountain-dedicated deputies. The full contract value is approximately $593,667.96. Supervisor Griner questioned the process and suggested the sheriff should be the one initiating staffing requests; Supervisors Robinson and Boots defended the data-driven county-initiated approach. Captain Sybert confirmed Rib Mountain is commercially heavy with high retail theft calls. The committee was told the contract must ultimately be ratified by the full county board.

discussions.item: Strategic Plan Public Survey
discussions.body: Board Vice Chair Boots briefly noted that the strategic plan survey is now open to the general public rather than targeted groups as in prior cycles, and encouraged committee members to urge constituents to participate. He indicated the committee would examine strategic plan results more closely in December after the budget process concludes.

discussions.item: 2027 Budget Overview for Committee Jurisdictions
discussions.body: Administrator Leonard highlighted key budget changes: the Clerk of Courts has anticipated new revenue from Wisconsin Act 179; the District Attorney's office faces a roughly $125,000 revenue reduction due to the state public defender's office lowering discovery payments statewide; the Medical Examiner's office abolished a deputy medical examiner position and created a senior administrative position, reducing overall expenditures; and the Sheriff's Office budget increase nearly accounts for all of the county's net new construction revenue, with $531,000 in attrition savings budgeted and increased rolling stock funding to address squad shortfalls from 2026. Supervisor Brandon asked about using opioid settlement funds to offset sheriff department costs such as Narcan and treatment programs; Leonard confirmed this is a viable strategy and favored a trust model for perpetual benefit, though no opioid settlement spending is included in the 2027 budget. Supervisor Tim requested cost information on flock cameras; Leonard indicated they are currently grant-funded but would confirm with the sheriff.

discussions.body: Supervisor Griner formally requested that drones and flock/Axon camera systems be placed on the next meeting agenda, including costs, number of units, locations, contractual terms, and early termination provisions. He expressed concern about undisclosed camera placements. Administrator Leonard noted a prior full presentation on license plate readers occurred at the August meeting. Sheriff Chad [last name inaudible] arrived during this discussion and was made aware of the request.

discussions.item: WDNR Final Decision on Corrosion Control Treatment (Ortho Phosphate)
discussions.body: Staff (identified as Eric and Scott) briefed the commission that the DNR issued a final decision in July requiring ortho phosphate to be operational no later than July 9, 2028. Staff noted a plan to install a temporary feed system before the permanent system is bid out in early 2027 to allow pipes to season ahead of required sampling. A commission member (Martins) asked whether progress on lead service line replacement could reduce or delay the ortho phosphate requirement; staff clarified it also benefits copper and in-home fixtures, so the requirement stands regardless. Staff noted a conflicting regulatory timeline — installation required by July 9, 2028 but sampling not due until June 9, 2029, leaving only one month rather than a full year. No action was requested; this was informational only.

discussions.item: Project Update: Headworks Screening and Crocker Street Lift Station
discussions.body: Ben reported that the wastewater headworks project is nearing substantial completion with an October 15 deadline expected to be met; a programming issue by Hydrodyne was resolved. The Crocker Street lift station project commenced September 22, with underground piping installed; Alliant Energy (WPS) is expected to complete new service this week and the lift station itself will be installed by the contractor (HOS) in spring with substantial completion by April 9, 2027. There was brief confusion among commissioners and staff about the exact street intersection (Crocker and [inaudible cross street]) before staff clarified it is on the northwest side.

discussions.item: PFAS Settlement Fund Expenditure Options for Capital Projects
discussions.body: Staff presented a spreadsheet of proposed capital projects highlighted for potential PFAS settlement funding use over the next five years, including the ortho phosphate installation, noting $1.67 million in EPA funding already secured with a remaining shortfall proposed to be covered by settlement funds rather than borrowing. Staff acknowledged the spreadsheet totals are not accurate and promised a corrected version for November. A commission member raised the DNR's 'clawback' position — requiring at least 50% of settlement funds be used to pay down the low-interest emerging contaminant loan used for the GAC system — and staff noted this is legally disputed by multiple municipalities. Commission member Hadley asked about the lead replacement contract; staff explained the DNR only permitted a three-year lock-in on construction pricing despite staff seeking five years, which commissioners criticized as an overreach. No action was taken; staff will return in November with corrected figures.

discussions.body: Ben presented the sole source justification for magnesium hydroxide, citing proven performance, the risk of chemistry instability when switching chemical vendors, and DNR compliance requirements. He noted a 5-cent per pound price increase but recommended continuing with the current supplier. Headley moved and Gellhar seconded. The motion passed on a voice vote with no opposition.

title: Community Life, Infrastructure and Public Property (CLIPP) Committee Meeting
overview: The Kronenwetter CLIPP Committee held its second review of the proposed 2027-2036 Capital Improvement Program (CIP), a 10-year plan totaling approximately $4.3 million in 2027 expenditures across roads, parks, utilities, public safety equipment, and facilities. No formal vote was taken on the CIP itself, as adoption is scheduled for the November 9 budget hearing; discussion focused on project priorities including Maple Ridge Road reconstruction, fire truck preordering timelines, lift station upgrades, a future water tower and well, and parks improvements at Bushga Park. The committee also briefly addressed a $1.2 million borrowing deadline of October 2027 and the fiscal implications of shifting $863,000 in TID 2 proceeds back to the village's general debt service.

discussions.item: 2027-2036 Capital Improvements Program - Overview
discussions.body: Village Administrator John presented the second draft of the 10-year CIP, noting the primary additions since the first draft were park committee items with cost estimates placed into specific years. He emphasized the 2027 year is the only year being formally adopted in the upcoming budget cycle, with 2028-2036 serving as a planning tool. The total proposed 2027 CIP expenditure is approximately $4.3 million spread across the general fund, capital projects fund, capital equipment fund, utility funds, and the park improvement fund. The administrator stressed the village has historically failed to invest in infrastructure — one employee noted it had been 26 years since the village last paved a road.

discussions.item: Fire Department Rescue Truck Preorder (2029)
discussions.body: The administrator noted the rescue/fire truck slotted for 2029 requires a formal commitment to preorder three to four years in advance, meaning an order placed now would likely not be received until 2030 or later. No down payment is required at order time, but the village board would need to sign a preorder agreement in a future budget year. The committee acknowledged this commitment does not need to be finalized in the next few months but cannot be deferred indefinitely without pushing delivery further out.

discussions.item: Maple Ridge Road Reconstruction
discussions.body: Trustee Myszka and President Joling identified Maple Ridge Road as the highest priority road project, noting it is the only village road with freeway access and the county recently improved adjacent county roads. Public Works Director Greg confirmed that core samples have been taken but a full engineering design is still needed; realistically, construction would begin in 2028 at the earliest. The administrator proposed potentially splitting the project across 2027 (engineering/design) and 2028 (construction), and noted that $1.2 million in leftover 2024 borrowing proceeds — which must be spent by October 2027 — could be committed to Maple Ridge. The committee discussed that approved bids from the village board may be sufficient to legally 'commit' those funds by the deadline. A question was raised about whether the steep hill section east of Spring could be graded down; Greg cautioned this would involve significant excavation costs, slope design, and potential DNR involvement.

discussions.item: Municipal Building Maintenance
discussions.body: Trustee [Patty Tukowski] raised concerns that only modest capital funds were set aside in 2027 for the municipal building despite known maintenance issues including roof leaks. The administrator acknowledged the building has suffered from years of inconsistent maintenance and explained that some repairs — such as heated roof tape and handicap entrance fixes — would be absorbed into the operational budget rather than the capital plan. He framed the CIP as a working document that will evolve as priorities shift.

discussions.item: Parks CIP Items and Fundraising Update
discussions.body: The parks committee additions, including playground equipment for Bushga Park and fencing for other parks, were incorporated into the CIP with 2027 borrowing projected at approximately $175,000, partially offset by $25,000 from the park improvement fund. Trustee [Patty Tukowski] noted the parks committee had unanimously recommended adding a zip line and rubber surface to Friendship Park for the 2029 improvement cycle; the administrator acknowledged this was not yet in the document and committed to adding it before the October 19-20 budget workshops. On fundraising, Trustee Myszka reported approximately $20,000 raised to date, including $1,348 from the 5K event and a $236 donation from the 50/50 raffle winner.

discussions.item: Sewer and Water Utility CIP Items
discussions.body: Public Works Director Greg detailed planned lift station upgrades (stations 5, 7, 9 panel replacements and generator additions), the removal of lift station 10 serving approximately 60 homes, and the in-progress removal of lift station 3 which uses a vacuum system prone to daily clogging. He highlighted the need for a vac/jet back truck (approximately $500,000) and a waste truck, both of which are dependent on the new garage being completed around February. The water utility section flagged a projected $11 million need for a new well and water tower, with the administrator cautioning this is a rough high estimate spread over multiple years and subject to a five-to-six-year Public Service Commission approval process. A potential TIF district was discussed as a way to offset water infrastructure costs, though TID 1 in the target area is severely distressed and cannot be overlaid with a new TID boundary.

discussions.item: Debt Service and Revenue Structure
discussions.body: The administrator explained that shifting $863,000 in TID 2 bond proceeds back to the village's general debt service — because the Flanner Jamerals project came in over budget and did not use those proceeds — will modestly increase the village's tax levy debt service obligation but allow TID 2 to close earlier, potentially releasing approximately $80 million in valuation and generating an estimated $250,000 annually in additional property tax revenue. Trustee [Paul Maja] recalled the administrator's earlier explanation that a significant drop in existing debt service around 2029 would help absorb new borrowing, which the administrator confirmed but noted the restructuring has reduced two prior projected drops to one drop of approximately $200,000 in 2029. For 2027, general obligation borrowing is proposed for only two projects: Bushga Park playground equipment and Maple Ridge Road, totaling approximately $1.8 million.

discussions.item: Highway Aid Formula Impact
discussions.body: The administrator noted that completing Kronenwetter Drive in 2025 ($2.2 million project) has already increased the village's annual state highway aid by over $50,000 for the 2027 budget year due to the state's three-year and six-year spending averages. He projected that continuing capital investments in roads and police staffing would further increase highway aid in 2028 and beyond, framing infrastructure investment as self-reinforcing from a revenue standpoint.

discussions.body: The committee noted the November 2nd meeting falls the day before the general election. Trustee [Patty Tukowski] indicated she would be working the election and would need to start at 6:30 a.m.; the committee briefly discussed moving the meeting start time to 5:30 p.m. with general agreement but no formal action. The administrator stated the November 2nd meeting would primarily provide a CIP update and possibly address the fire truck commitment timeline. Trustee Myszka requested a follow-up on the park bricks project for a future agenda.

discussions.body: Alder Swansky moved to approve the minutes of the preceding meeting. Alder True Blood seconded. The minutes were approved unanimously on a voice vote with no corrections or additions.

discussions.item: 3A: Award of Bid for Pleasant View Park Ash Tree Removal
discussions.body: Parks staff Jamie and city forester John presented the situation: emerald ash borer infestation has affected the majority of ash trees at Pleasant View Park, particularly around the sledding hill. Only one bid was received from Shriber Logging at $5,500, which covers mobilization costs as the timber market is depressed following closure of a local pulp mill. Staff noted the removal will significantly change the park's wooded appearance but that inaction would leave hazardous dead trees threatening the sledding hill amenity. Alder True Blood asked what would happen without action and received confirmation the park's appearance will change regardless. The $5,500 will come from the urban forestry/emerald ash borer dedicated budget. Alder Swansky inquired about the likelihood of additional bids; staff expressed confidence no other bidders would come forward given the small parcel size and city constraints. The committee voted unanimously to award the bid.

discussions.item: 3B: Amendment of the Junior Achievement Agreement (Wangard Property)
discussions.body: Patrick Gatman from city planning and Vinnie presented an amendment to terminate Junior Achievement's rights to construct a 'champions area' in Area B of the Wangard property agreement. This cleanup was prompted by a certified survey map process for the property. Junior Achievement confirmed they have no intention to build there in the future. The committee approved the amendment unanimously on a voice vote after no substantive debate.

discussions.item: 4A: Purchase of County-Owned Parkland on 28th Avenue for Future City Park
discussions.body: Jamie presented a county-owned parcel on 28th Avenue, originally purchased in 2006 for a highway corridor that was never built, now offered to the city. The roughly 3-acre parcel was originally labeled 'private park' in a 1974 development. Staff reported after a site visit that the land is very rocky, steeply graded, and largely undevelopable except for a small fill area potentially suitable for a playground. The city's park dedication fund holds approximately $536,064 that could be used for purchase. One committee member stated they would not personally support the purchase given the department's existing workload and the site's limited development potential. The matter was deferred to closed session for further deliberation on potential purchase price and interest.

discussions.item: 4B: Park Updates – Athletic Park, Oak Island, River Edge Trail, Riverlife
discussions.body: Jamie announced the skate park is now complete and is working with donor families on a plaque unveiling. Alder Swansky asked about the cost of ongoing vandalism to Riverlife Park restrooms; Jamie noted the locking mechanisms on the south-side bathrooms have been difficult to replace due to jamming of the electronic locks and said a cost summary would be provided at the next meeting.

discussions.item: 5A: Hearing – Appeal of Tree Assessment Fee, 4011 Stone Ridge Drive
discussions.body: The committee conducted a formal quasi-judicial hearing on homeowner Jonathan Mafam's appeal of a city forester fee for damaging a city tree during unpermitted excavation. City plumbing inspector Dennis Keski testified that he found trenching had been done without an excavation or lateral permit and that as of the morning of the meeting no permit had been obtained. City forester John Kahan, a board-certified master arborist, testified the tree was losing leaves early due to root damage caused by the trenching, that the permit process would have identified a safer route or offered tree removal for a $550 fee, and that a pre-existing seam/occlusion in the tree was unrelated to the dieback. Mafam testified he purchased the home in September 2024, suffered a flooded finished basement and $30,000 in losses in the first spring, and was trying to install a French drain system; he stated he did not know he needed a permit, did not know the tree was a city tree, his contractor abandoned the job incomplete, and he was asking for leniency. He disputed John's characterization of his visit to the property. After testimony and committee questions, Alder Slonsky moved to adjourn into closed session for deliberation; the motion passed on a 4-0 roll call vote.

title: Finance Committee Budget Session #1
overview: The Wausau Finance Committee held its first of four budget workshop sessions for the 2027 city budget on October 5, 2026. The proposed budget includes a total city levy of $40.63 million, up $2.5 million (6.76%) from the prior year, with $1.45 million of the increase driven by a voter-approved referendum. The session covered high-level budget impacts, public works, motorpool, water/wastewater, and parks department budgets, with significant discussion around motorpool funding shortfalls, health insurance cost pressures, and the need for revenue diversification.

discussions.item: Mayor's High-Level Budget Overview
discussions.body: Mayor Doug Diny presented the top-line 2027 budget: $40.63 million total city levy, up $2.5 million from 2026, with an assessed tax rate of $9.24 per thousand. He noted that $1.45 million of the increase (3.8%) is attributable to the voter-approved referendum, and the remaining 1.9% stems from operational factors. Directors were directed to seek a 2% decrease in cost-to-continue expenses; four positions are being held vacant (~$410,000 in savings). A new city administrator position at $150,000 is included, envisioned to review and implement recommendations from a pending citywide audit. No new fees are proposed, consistent with the council's stated opposition to regressive fees.

discussions.item: Finance Director Budget Presentation — Revenues, Levy, and Assessed Value
discussions.body: Finance Director Maryanne detailed that computer aid came in at $557,000 versus a budgeted $513,000, yielding approximately $44,000 in additional revenue — a modification not yet reflected in the budget book. She noted assessed value is estimated at 1% growth pending mid-October confirmation, meaning the tax rate could shift. Impact on a median home is estimated at $99.73. She also distributed a Forward Analytics report showing Marathon County's net new construction is covering only about half of CPI growth since 2010, illustrating structural revenue constraints. The garbage contract increase of approximately $291,000 — absorbed into the levy rather than passed to ratepayers — was cited as a key cost pressure.

discussions.item: Position Vacancies and HR Position Authorization
discussions.body: An alderperson (identified as Vicki in context) raised a concern that an additional HR position budgeted at $100,000 had not been fully authorized by the council, noting she voted against it previously and was unaware of it returning for a vote. Maryanne and other officials explained the position is being brought back at the HR committee meeting the following week, and that it had previously been approved with the understanding it would be filled after a new director was hired. The vacancies held open include: one downtown police officer FTE (previously foundation-funded), one assistant city attorney FTE, a half-year fire division chief/inspection lieutenant FTE, a DPW surveyor half-FTE, a parks administrative coordinator half-FTE, and a CCITC project manager FTE.

discussions.item: Public Works Department Budget
discussions.body: DPW Director Eric presented the public works budget, which decreased roughly 4% overall. Discussion focused on leaf pickup operations — clarifying the city never conducted two full collections but eliminated the two-phase map that caused public confusion. Alderperson Watson raised a concern about significant reductions in contractual services (~$80,000) relative to the DPW request, with Eric noting the cuts were made line-by-line with the mayor and finance director and that the city surveyor position remains unfilled due to lack of qualified applicants. Fee structure was discussed, with committee members noting inspection and land-use permit fees remained flat while animal licensing fees were proposed to increase — a disparity questioned by at least one alderperson.

discussions.item: Motorpool Budget and Mercury Audit
discussions.body: The motorpool discussion revealed a recurring structural shortfall: departments requiring motorpool services cannot afford full cost recovery through their levy-funded budgets. In 2025, actual motorpool charges to the general fund totaled $5.6 million against budgeted amounts of $4.1 million, leaving a $1.4 million gap partially covered by investment income ($370,000) and departmental savings. Alderperson Hanie questioned how many Mercury audit recommendations had been implemented; fleet staff confirmed four were addressed (hiring a fleet analyst, reassessing rental rates, increasing staffing, reducing fleet age) but acknowledged the core problem is that departments cannot afford the equipment they need. Eric argued the city must diversify revenue — specifically citing a wheel tax, stormwater utility, and converting garbage to a special charge — to sustainably fund motorpool. The aerial truck replacement was flagged as a deferred need: lead time is 24 months for a standard model or up to 51 months for a custom unit; a vendor offered a ~$200,000 discount for prepayment, which the city historically does not do.

discussions.item: Water and Wastewater Utility Budgets
discussions.body: Eric and Maryanne presented both utility budgets, which remained relatively flat year-over-year. A notable item is $1.667 million in congressionally directed spending originally earmarked for granular activated carbon replacements; the EPA ruled that use ineligible (classifying it as operations rather than capital), so the city intends to redirect the funds toward an ortho phosphate corrosion control system required by mandate to be operational by 2028. Staffing increases in both water and wastewater utilities were confirmed as previously approved. Other financing sources in both funds represent borrowing for capital projects, including $6 million for public-side lead service line replacement.

discussions.item: Parks Department Budget
discussions.body: Parks Director presented a 2027 proposed budget only $18,652 over the 2026 adopted budget, achieved through operational reductions approved by the parks committee: rotating pool schedule (two pools open weekdays, all three on weekends), elimination of the downtown flower basket program from the operating budget (potentially to be funded from room tax at committee's discretion), and reduction of WARF docks from seven to five. Fee increases and adding the Brockmere Park main building to the rental schedule contributed to revenue offsets. No significant capital improvement projects are planned for 2027; focus will shift to deferred maintenance. An Oak Island tennis court renovation will be pursued through a Community Development Block Grant. The skate park refurbishment was cited as complete. Discussion included creative ideas for flower basket sponsorships modeled on programs in Merrill and Napa Valley.

discussions.item: Closing Discussion — Health Insurance, Asphalt Overlay, Animal Control, Block Cameras
discussions.body: Mayor Diny noted asphalt overlay was increased from $600,000 to $800,000, citing that inflation-adjusted road spending is less than half of levels from 10-12 years ago. He flagged health insurance as a critical long-term concern: a 9.6% increase this year (~$450,000), with a family plan costing the city approximately $35,000 annually (88% city share), on a trajectory to double in 6-7 years. An alderperson raised the 3% COLA plus 1.5% step increase compounding as a further concern. An alderperson indicated intent to propose an amendment related to animal control fund levy independence and requested data ahead of Tuesday's police budget session. Another committee member flagged the $50,000 block camera contract as controversial and subject to scrutiny on Tuesday.

title: Board Special Meeting
overview: The Marathon County Board held a special meeting on October 1, 2026 to consider Resolution 55-26, directing Alliant Energy to submit a draft proposal addressing community concerns about the Hub City Wind Project by November 1st. The resolution passed, though not unanimously, signaling the board's intent to assess Alliant's willingness to negotiate without formally committing to a joint developer agreement. The meeting also included announcements about the county's upcoming budget process and a public strategic plan survey.

discussions.item: Staff presentation: Options for county engagement with Alliant Energy
discussions.body: County Administrator Lori McSkimmons presented a table of four options for the board: (1) negotiating a Joint Developer Agreement (JDA), estimated cost up to $20,000; (2) intervening in the PSC permitting process, estimated $75,000–$200,000+; (3) adopting a moratorium, cost unknown and noted as likely unenforceable on a 100-megawatt project; and (4) appealing the PSC's decision after issuance, estimated $20,000–$50,000. She noted PSC staff confirmed no intervention has ever stopped a project and that Columbia County's similar moratorium effort was sent back to committee. She emphasized options are not mutually exclusive and that the county could not file for intervention until after Alliant submits its formal PSC application, which could come as early as mid-December 2026.

discussions.item: Resolution 55-26 — Hub City Wind Project engagement with Alliant Energy
discussions.body: Supervisor Robinson, who authored the resolution and chaired the alternative energy advisory committee, explained it does not commit the county to a JDA but rather asks Alliant Energy to submit a draft proposal addressing community concerns by November 1st, after which the board would evaluate next steps. Supervisor Dickinson expressed strong opposition, stating he would not vote for anything that moved toward a JDA and questioned whether Alliant would engage in good faith. Supervisor Leur raised concerns that the resolution puts the county in a reactive position and called for an energy summit to address broader regional energy policy. Supervisor Ritter, Supervisor Nath, Supervisor Rosenberg, and Supervisor Robinson defended the resolution as a proactive first step to gauge Alliant's willingness to address constituents' concerns on issues including decommissioning, setbacks, emergency response, property values, and health impacts. The resolution passed but was noted by Chair Gibbs as not unanimous.

discussions.item: Announcements: Budget process and strategic plan survey
discussions.body: Supervisor Robinson announced that the county administrator's proposed budget was accepted by the Human Resources Finance Property Committee and is now the county board's budget. Key dates include: amendment submissions by October 9th, committee authorization for publication on October 12th, a public hearing on November 2nd at 3:00 p.m., and full board budget adoption on November 10th. Chair Gibbs noted the public hearing was moved to 3:00 p.m. on November 2nd to avoid conflicts with Election Day on November 3rd. McSkimmons announced that a public survey on the county's strategic plan — narrowing 20 objectives down to 10 priorities — would open October 2nd and run through October 23rd.

title: Village Board Meeting
overview: The Kronenwetter Village Board held its September 28, 2026 meeting, approving the Green Tree Trails subdivision preliminary plan (60+ one-acre lots with private wells and septic) unanimously after significant public comment and board discussion, and also approved a zoning text amendment allowing zero-lot-line (twin home) structures. The board received extensive budget previews including a $56,000 increase in state transportation aid for 2027, a proposed $39/year garbage fee increase driven by diesel fuel surcharges, and a 10-year Capital Improvement Plan with two 2027 borrowing projects: Maple Ridge Road and Bushna Park improvements.

discussions.item: Public Comment - Green Tree Trails Subdivision
discussions.body: Three residents spoke during public comment. Guy Friedel of Ruby Drive argued the village should pursue smaller lots with municipal sewer and water to double the tax base, suggesting referral to the utilities and APC committees and the use of special assessments. Marie Kramer of Highway 153 questioned the wisdom of private wells and septic given groundwater concerns and proximity to existing sewer service, saying 'we're walking backwards.' Joanne Mansel of Pine Road asked about minimum lot size and frontage requirements and stated she disagrees with more density, saying 'I think 60 homes is plenty' and that one-acre lots would be appropriate for the area.

discussions.item: Administrator Report
discussions.body: Administrator Jim Dabel announced the new Village Clerk will start October 19 and will be introduced at that time, noting strong experienced applicants. He reported FedEx ground-breaking is expected by mid-to-late November, which is significant for TID 1 revenues. He also praised DPW staff for site preparation work behind the municipal building, saving significant money, and noted budget materials in the packet are a precursor to the 2027 budget process.

discussions.item: DPW Report - Green Acres Road School Bus Turnaround
discussions.body: DPW Director Greg [last name inaudible] reported that a resident's concern about school buses not being able to turn around on Green Acres Road is being investigated; the existing turnaround used by plow and garbage trucks was found too small for school buses. He is coordinating with the school district and bus company to evaluate options, including a possible hammerhead turnaround, but noted the village does not control the bus company contract. Trustee Solheim asked for an update by the next meeting. The director also reported that the new employee parking garage is on track, with permits approved and concrete work expected to begin within a week and a half.

discussions.item: Finance Director Report - Per-Capita Spending Comparisons
discussions.body: Finance Director John Jacobs presented a detailed comparison of Kronenwetter against nine other north-central Wisconsin communities using 2024 state data. Key findings: Kronenwetter is near the bottom for per-capita spending on streets ($147/person), fire ($47/person), and police ($163/person); property taxes are the lowest at $317/person but 84% comes from residential versus 60-70% for peer communities. Jacobs emphasized the need for commercial and manufacturing diversification, noting TID 1 and TID 2 as critical tools, and that the FedEx distribution center could stop the $100,000-$120,000 annual general fund bleeding into TID 1.

discussions.item: Green Tree Trails Subdivision Preliminary Plan
discussions.body: Community Development Director Nathan Sandwick presented the preliminary plan for approximately 60+ one-acre lots with private wells and septic systems, noting unanimous planning commission approval in June. Board discussion focused on the history of the property (turned down nine times under previous developer), the decision not to extend municipal sewer and water due to costs over $1.6 million, and the compromise of one-acre lots meeting septic minimums. Concerns were raised about traffic on Nick Avenue, which will be gated as emergency access only. Trustee Mishka moved to approve, seconded by Trustee Coyle; the motion passed 7-0.

discussions.item: Text Amendment Chapter 520 - Zero Lot Line Structures
discussions.body: Sandwick presented a zoning ordinance amendment to allow twin homes (zero-lot-line structures) where duplexes are currently permitted on 20,000 square foot parcels, enabling each half to be individually owned. Trustee Lesniak moved to approve, seconded by Trustee Stowell. No notable debate was recorded; the amendment passed 7-0 on a roll call vote.

discussions.item: Budget Preview - Garbage Fees and Debt
discussions.body: Jacobs reported a $56,000 increase in state transportation aid for the 2027 budget. On garbage fees, he presented scenarios driven by diesel fuel surcharges in the Harder's contract; with diesel exceeding $6.50/gallon, the village faces a $57,000 shortfall in 2026. The planning figure recommended by APC of $6.25/gallon would raise household garbage fees from $228 to approximately $267.24 per year (a $39 increase). Administrator Dabel recommended using $6.25 as the planning factor for the budget while monitoring prices. Jacobs also outlined a debt restructuring plan to shift $863,000 in unused TID 2 bond proceeds to the capital project fund, reducing TID 2 debt and freeing resources, with the tax levy absorbing a small $12,000 increase in annual debt service.

discussions.item: 10-Year Capital Improvement Plan (CIP) - 2027 Projects
discussions.body: Jacobs presented the second review of the 10-year CIP, emphasizing only 43% of the $30 million plan relies on general obligation borrowing. For 2027, two borrowing projects are proposed: Maple Ridge Road (total ~$2.9M, with $1.2M already on hand reducing new borrowing to ~$1.7M) and Bushna Park improvements (~$25,000 from the park fund plus borrowed remainder). Board discussion touched on building security upgrades including key fob access (~$100,000 estimate) and cameras, audio-visual improvements to the meeting room, and the need for a long-range plan for municipal center maintenance. Jacobs noted the plan is a fluid document to be reviewed annually.

title: Comprehensive Plan Steering Committee
overview: The Village of Weston held a joint Comprehensive Plan Steering Committee meeting of the Village Board of Trustees and Planning Commission to review progress on a 10-year comprehensive plan update. Consultant Mark Roers of MD Roers Consulting presented survey results, stakeholder interview findings, draft vision statements, and preliminary chapter goals and initiatives covering land use, economic development, housing, transportation, and intergovernmental cooperation. The committee reached consensus on using draft vision statement 'C' for public presentation and set a public workshop for November 12, 2024, from 5 to 7 p.m.

Roll call

discussions.item: Public Comment
discussions.body: No speakers appeared in person or online. An emailed written comment from resident Sarah Prather regarding an indoor playground, addressed to Jennifer Higgins, Jamie Sean, Mark Roers, and Audrey Webster, was distributed to the board. President Maloney noted it would be entered into the record and included in the packet.

discussions.item: Meetings and Milestones Update
discussions.body: Consultant Mark Roers outlined the comprehensive plan update process, noting that a community survey drew nearly 700 respondents, stakeholder interviews reached 24 identified contacts with 10 completing interviews, and a young adult questionnaire targeting ages 20–35 yielded 48 responses via social media. Roers explained the plan is divided into three volumes, with Volume 2 (Vision and Directions) as the current focus, targeting a public hearing by March. The board noted that 48 young adult responses exceeded the typical weekly newsletter poll response of about 27.

discussions.item: Stakeholder Interview and Young Adult Questionnaire Results
discussions.body: Roers summarized cross-cutting themes from all input channels: safety ranked as the top community value across all age groups; residents want more retail, restaurants, and groceries; interviewees emphasized need for workforce housing, particularly entry-level single-family homes and duplexes over large apartment complexes; and intergovernmental respondents favored expanding collaborative services while keeping Weston's suburban character distinct from larger neighbors. Young adults specifically cited school quality, parks, family orientation, housing affordability, and indoor recreation as priorities.

discussions.item: Draft Vision Statement Review
discussions.body: Roers presented three vision statement options (A from 2016, B from the recent strategic plan, and C newly drafted by Roers with AI assistance). Pre-meeting homework showed C received seven votes, A received one, and B received none. Discussion focused on tweaking C: Trustee Brent Olson suggested removing the word 'thoughtfully' from 'Weston will grow thoughtfully,' with others suggesting 'intentionally' as a substitute; one reviewer had suggested removing 'and welcoming' from the opening line, which drew pushback; another suggested adding 'can' language in multiple places, which was debated. The committee reached consensus to bring a refined version of C to the November 12 public workshop.

discussions.item: Community Growth Map and Geographic Vision
discussions.body: Roers presented a generalized growth pattern map highlighting three mixed-use corridors (Scoffield Avenue, County Road X/Camp Phillips Road, and Weston Avenue) and identified a potential third interchange at Ryan Street as a priority transportation and land use initiative. Trustee or commissioner Gary Garn noted that Marathon County has a no-trucking restriction on Highway J south of Weston Avenue, which would need to be addressed for future southern industrial expansion. Extended discussion covered a potential bridge crossing north from the Caleb Drive area of Sandy Lane subdivision to improve connectivity, with staff noting the Oakclair River floodplain narrows at that point and that the northeast annexation area is known to the town chair.

discussions.item: Hyperscale Data Center Policy
discussions.body: Roers recommended a draft initiative to 'support more industrial development while restricting hyperscale projects,' defining hyperscale as typically requiring 100 or more acres. He cited the DeForest example of a 1,500-acre proposal that was rejected and noted concerns about power consumption, long construction periods, land obsolescence, and community division. Board members expressed agreement with establishing a policy and raised questions about when to address related issues such as solar fields, wind turbines, and EV chargers. Roers noted solar field incentives are diminishing and cited a 2,500-acre proposal near Cambridge. The committee appeared to support the proposed policy direction without a formal vote.

discussions.item: Housing Chapter and State Law Initiatives
discussions.body: Roers outlined new state-level tools including a pay-as-you-go TIF district specifically for residential development on lots no larger than 7,500 square feet with house size caps (1,500 sq ft single-story, 2,000 sq ft two-story), aimed at starter homes. He also noted infrastructure reimbursement mechanisms for developers and referenced the Truth in Planning law requiring communities to plan for sufficient housing land and be open to rezoning consistent with their plans. The board asked whether developer-fronted infrastructure costs could deter development; Roers said hybrid approaches are possible and that lenders are generally familiar with these structures.

discussions.item: Tax Incremental Financing — New Generation
discussions.body: Roers explained that TID No. 1, the larger of Weston's two active districts, will close at year-end, creating room to establish new, smaller, project-specific TIDs. He cited DeForest's model of seven active TIDs and described the shift toward pay-as-you-go (PAYGO) structures where developers front infrastructure costs and are reimbursed through incremental tax revenue, closing districts faster. No vote was taken.

discussions.item: Pre-Meeting Initiative Prioritization Results
discussions.body: Staff reported results of a pre-meeting homework exercise in which board and commission members ranked draft initiatives. 'Continue existing and pursue more opportunities for collaborative services' ranked first with six votes. Tied for second with five votes each were 'maintain the function and condition of Weston's roads' and 'help expand and attract retailers, restaurants, grocers, and industries in targeted sectors.' Tied for third with four votes each were 'phase growth according to utility, road, stormwater, and service capacity,' 'reinvest in older neighborhoods and housing,' and 'update Weston's five-year strategic plan.'

discussions.item: Shaping Weston's Tomorrow Public Workshop
discussions.body: The committee confirmed a public workshop titled 'Shaping Weston's Tomorrow' for November 12, 2024, from 5 to 7 p.m. Roers outlined plans for interactive small-group discussions rather than a lecture format, organized around topics such as transportation and natural resources. A board member requested a poster be created within 22 hours to publicize the event at a community event the following evening; staff confirmed they could produce one using Canva. Roers encouraged board members who attend to listen rather than actively participate in small groups.

overview: The Village of Weston Parks and Recreation Committee met on September 30, 2024, covering updates on Kennedy Park renovations, the Muler Park master plan, aquatic center repairs, and a farmers market end-of-season survey. The committee voted to conduct a fall farmers market survey with an added question about Kennedy Park usage, and approved moving forward with an updated aquatic center facility evaluation.

discussions.item: Approval of minutes from August 24th meeting
discussions.body: Minutes were moved by Scott and seconded by Roger. The committee approved them unanimously on a voice vote.

discussions.item: Public comments
discussions.body: A resident named Grace, of 603 Jessica Street, offered three comments: she thanked committee members for asking probing questions about the ice rink proposal at Kennedy Park; she requested a more formal, structured presentation on Kennedy Park's progress and future plans, rather than informal monthly updates; and she asked whether Prohaska Park has a sign, bathrooms, and regular mowing. Staff confirmed the park has a sign and that only the walking trails are mowed, with no formal amenity area.

discussions.item: Update on Kennedy Park renovation
discussions.body: Staff reported that contractors are scheduled to arrive the following week to address touch-up paint on poles, crack block and missing mortar, dugout door adjustments, sod restoration from irrigation leak repairs, and irrigation system restoration. Lights are scheduled for delivery the week of the 19th and will be installed immediately upon delivery. A representative from Friends of Kennedy Park said there were no additional updates. No action was taken.

discussions.item: Update on Muler Park master plan
discussions.body: Staff reported that following the September 3rd public input meeting, the consultant revised the concept design to add tennis and basketball courts and relocated the shelter near the pickleball/basketball/tennis area. Public feedback on the concept was largely positive with few suggested changes. Three emails were received requesting that any future playground addition be fully ADA-accessible. Staff noted playground equipment at Muler was intentionally excluded from the seven-playground replacement project due to its relative newness (installed 2007), but replacement would be planned if the master plan moves forward. A cost estimate is being prepared and will return to the committee for approval or denial. No action was taken.

discussions.item: Update on aquatic center repairs
discussions.body: Staff reported the contractor moved up their schedule and now expects to begin work at the aquatic center the week of October 5th, earlier than the previously anticipated late October window. Work includes leak detection, a valve and motor replacement, and winterization. Staff is preparing the mechanical room for the contractor's arrival. Electrical and commercial pool permits through the village are being processed. No action was taken.

discussions.item: Discussion and action on farmers market end-of-season survey
discussions.body: Staff presented revised survey questions for a second end-of-season farmers market survey, noting the first survey was issued too early in the season. The proposed survey has nine questions including an open-ended final question. Committee members discussed whether to include a vendor-specific survey; staff noted the existing survey already asks respondents to identify as vendors. A committee member suggested adding a 10th question asking how respondents otherwise use Kennedy Park, which received broad support. Trustee Beck, participating online, supported conducting the survey now while the season is fresh. The committee voted to proceed with the survey, to be released around October 1st and run approximately 30 days.

discussions.item: Discussion on collecting feedback regarding ice skating rinks at Kennedy Park
discussions.body: Staff recapped discussions from March and April about the cost and usage of the Kennedy Park outdoor ice rink, noting that since the warming house closed in 2019, attendance tracking has been limited but staff observe regular use. Cost to maintain the rink is primarily utilities—approximately $800 in water usage annually—since labor costs remain fixed regardless. Committee members debated whether a public survey would be useful, with concern that respondents without context might vote against a low-cost community amenity. One member noted the rink is the only full-size outdoor hockey rink (200x85 feet) in the area. The committee reached a consensus not to conduct a standalone ice rink survey, but agreed to add a question about Kennedy Park usage to the existing farmers market survey. No formal vote was taken on the ice rink item.

discussions.item: Discussion and action on completing an updated aquatic center evaluation
discussions.body: Staff noted the last aquatic center evaluation was completed in 2016 at just under $7,000, and that significant capital expenditures have followed, including over $102,000 in leak repairs this year and another motor and valve replacement project exceeding $100,000. Staff estimated a new evaluation could cost $7,000–$12,000. A committee member raised the question of whether to wait given ongoing discussions about a possible pool partnership with the Everest School District, which recently mailed a facilities survey to residents. After discussion, the committee agreed that an evaluation could actually inform the partnership decision. A motion was made and seconded to proceed with the aquatic center evaluation; the motion was approved unanimously on a voice vote.

publicComment: One speaker offered public comment: Grace, of 603 Jessica Street. She thanked committee members for questioning the ice rink proposal at Kennedy Park at a previous meeting, requested more formal and structured presentations on Kennedy Park's progress and future direction (including from Friends of Kennedy Park), and asked about the status of Prohaska Park—specifically whether it has a sign, bathrooms, and is regularly mowed. Staff answered that it does have a sign, and that only the walking trails are mowed. A person identified as David joined the meeting online but declined to offer public comment when invited.

title: Police & Fire Commission Meeting
overview: The Wausau Police & Fire Commission met on September 28, 2026, conducting organizational business including electing a new vice president and secretary after Commissioner Tom Garver's departure from the commission. The meeting featured substantive updates from Fire Deputy Chief Justin and Police Chief Barnes covering apprenticeship hiring, budget constraints, the proposed UW campus acquisition, and the department's Flock license plate recognition camera system.

discussions.item: Public Comment – Tom Garver Farewell
discussions.body: Outgoing Commissioner Tom Garver, of 4620 Huntington Court, addressed the commission to mark his departure, citing 'circumstances beyond our control' requiring him to leave. He praised the commission's culture of hiring for character, commended department leadership, and expressed confidence in newly appointed commissioners. The chair noted Garver was recently inducted into the Army Sports Hall of Fame in September for his hockey career at West Point, where he holds the program's all-time wins record with 75 victories.

discussions.item: Election of Commission Vice President
discussions.body: With Garver's departure creating a vacancy in the vice president role, Commissioner Lisa nominated Veta Perkins (referred to as 'V') for vice president. Another commissioner moved to close nominations, and the motion to elect Perkins as VP passed unanimously. The chair also appointed Lisa as commission secretary without a formal vote, stating it was an appointment rather than an election.

discussions.item: Approval of August 24 Meeting Minutes
discussions.body: The chair asked for corrections to the August 24 minutes. None were raised. A motion to approve was made and seconded, passing unanimously with no discussion.

discussions.item: Fire Department Monthly Update
discussions.body: Fire Deputy Chief Justin reported nine new apprentices starting that day from a pool of 45 applicants, calling the field strong. He noted six current vacancies in the department; seven candidates were interviewed for firefighter-paramedic positions but only two will advance to the PFC for approval, leaving four vacancies remaining. He also highlighted new scheduling software intended to reduce administrative burden on battalion chiefs and reduce mandatory overtime, new training software in development, a successful DEA audit of the department's controlled substances practices led by Division Chief Matt Tormolan, and the widely publicized rescue of two occupants of a small aircraft that made an emergency water landing in Lake Wausau after dark, one of whom was later identified as a gubernatorial candidate.

discussions.item: Police Department Monthly Update
discussions.body: Chief Barnes reported that a recent police hiring process drew 40 applicants after targeted social media advertising in Wisconsin, and described the preliminary interview pool as the best the department has seen. He said the department anticipates hiring eight or nine officers in the next 12 months due to three current openings and five or six expected retirements. On budget, Barnes said the department is leaving two positions unfilled through August to meet required savings, and that the overall authorized FTE count is dropping from 81 to 80 in 2027 as foundation funding for one of two downtown homeless outreach officer positions expires — the city will fund one position and the other will simply not be backfilled. Barnes also updated the commission on the city's proposal to acquire the UW-Wausau campus, noting the city is seeking six months for due diligence and has requested a $50,000 budget modification for expert consultants; a first council vote failed due to lack of quorum and one abstention, but the finance committee has since approved the modification and it will return to the full council. Barnes addressed the Flock license plate recognition camera system, stating the department owns 20 cameras at $50,000 per year on a five-year contract, that Flock does not sell city data, and that data is deleted after 30 days; a formal presentation to the PFC is planned for October or November.

discussions.item: Deputy Chief Promotional Process
discussions.body: Chief Barnes outlined the timeline for selecting a new deputy chief: letters of interest and resumes were due October 2nd, officer listening sessions with the commission (without Barnes or Fire Chief Todd present) are planned for mid-October, candidate written assignments and interviews with Barnes are set for November 11th, and PFC interviews and a vote are planned for mid-to-late November with a January 17th promotional date. Commissioners discussed whether the PFC interviews could be held during the regular November 23rd meeting; Barnes said it was feasible but noted interviews could take several hours and might require a reduced agenda.

He praised department leadership, emphasized the importance of hiring for character, and thanked his fellow commissioners.

title: Public Health & Safety Committee Meeting
overview: The Wausau Public Health & Safety Committee held a brief meeting on September 28th, approving minutes, a batch of license applications, and two 90-day liquor license extensions for businesses under construction. Two discussion items — an update on the Marathon County/City of Wausau homelessness response framework and the August tavern activities report — were tabled to the October 19th meeting due to the absence of scheduled presenters.

4A: Update on Marathon County and City of Wausau foundational framework for homelessness response and strategic plan development
4B: Tavern activities report from August 2026
Adjournment

discussions.item: Minutes of preceding meetings
discussions.body: The chair asked if members had reviewed the regular and special Public Health & Safety Committee minutes. No revisions or questions were raised. Alder Slonsky moved to approve and Alder Watson seconded; the motion passed unanimously.

discussions.item: 3A: Various license applications
discussions.body: The chair noted no applications were being denied and asked if members were in agreement to approve the batch. No discussion occurred. Alder Watson moved to approve and Alder True Blood seconded; the motion passed unanimously.

discussions.item: 3B: 90-day extension for 2510 Delhi and Bakery (2510 Stewart Avenue)
discussions.body: A staff member provided context that the bakery had experienced construction delays but expected to open within the 90-day extension period. No objections were raised. Alder Slonsky moved to approve and Alder Watson seconded; the motion passed unanimously.

discussions.item: 3C: 90-day extension for True North #855 (4611 Stewart Avenue)
discussions.body: A staff member noted receiving an email that morning indicating True North expected to be done by November 1st, within the 90-day window. Alder Slonsky moved to approve and Alder True Blood seconded; the motion passed unanimously.

discussions.item: 4A: Update on Marathon County and City of Wausau homelessness response framework
discussions.body: The scheduled presenter was absent. Committee members questioned whether the item was related to the homelessness task force and whether the presenter would be Tracy or Megan Bernett, described as the new health coordinator. The chair indicated no motion was needed and the item would be carried over; a committee member suggested asking Alder Larson to place it on the October agenda.

discussions.item: 4B: Tavern activities report from August 2026
discussions.body: No presenter was available to report. A committee member noted there were items of potential public interest, including 'pretty intense demerit points' addressed during the month, and suggested circling back next month when staff could be present to answer questions. The item was deferred to the October 19th meeting.

title: Annual Meeting Budget Hearing
overview: Based on the published agenda, the Wausau School District's Annual Meeting and Budget Hearing on September 28, 2026, was scheduled to address the 2026-2027 proposed budget, consider eight resolutions for voter approval including tax levy measures, and conduct routine annual business. The meeting was expected to include a State of the District presentation from Superintendent Bushman and a public hearing regarding an early start date for the 2027-2028 school year.

discussions.item: Public Hearing for Resolution Requesting Starting School Prior to September 1 for 2027-2028
discussions.body: The board was scheduled to hold a public hearing on a resolution that would request approval to begin the 2027-2028 school year prior to September 1. This hearing provided an opportunity for community members to comment on the proposed early start date before any action was taken.

discussions.item: State of the District Presentation
discussions.body: Superintendent Bushman was scheduled to present a brief State of the District update, providing an overview of district operations, accomplishments, and challenges for stakeholders and board members.

discussions.item: Treasurer's Report
discussions.body: The board was scheduled to receive the Treasurer's Report for June 2026, which would provide financial information regarding the district's fiscal status heading into the new budget year.

discussions.item: Other Post Employment Benefits Report
discussions.body: The board was scheduled to review the OPEB Annual Report for June 2026, addressing the district's obligations and liabilities related to post-employment benefits for retirees.

discussions.item: Review Proposed 2026-2027 Budget
discussions.body: Dr. Elizabeth Channel, Assistant Superintendent of Operations, was scheduled to present the proposed 2026-2027 budget to the board and electorate. The presentation was expected to include a comprehensive budget booklet with detailed financial information and a summary presentation in Canva format.

discussions.item: New Business - Eight Motions for Electorate Consideration
discussions.body: The board was scheduled to consider eight different resolutions for voter approval, including measures addressing tax levies for the general fund, community service fund, and debt service fund; school lunch operations; school board member reimbursement and salaries; real estate authorizations; and establishment of the 2027 annual meeting date.

publicComment: A public comment period was included on this agenda as part of the public hearing for the resolution requesting an early school start date for 2027-2028.
